items.title: Watch: Bizarre Tentacled UFO Filmed Floating Near Major U.S. Military Base; Witnesses Speak
items.content_text:
Watch: Bizarre Tentacled UFO Filmed Floating Near Major U.S. Military Base; Witnesses Speak

A bizarre, jellyfish-shaped object with dangling tentacles has been captured on video hovering in the skies near a major U.S. military installation, leaving witnesses baffled by what they saw, the Daily Mail reports.

The mysterious sighting occurred June 15 in Anchorage, Alaska, in the direction of Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, home to America's formidable F-22 Raptor fighter jets.

Sara Jane Osborn was photographing a rainbow with her husband, Pete, when she noticed an unusual black-and-silver object floating above the distant treetops. At first, Osborn thought it was an insect. "I was annoyed, because I was like, is that a mosquito?" she recalled in an interview with the Daily Mail.

However, the object appeared much farther away, sporting several tentacle-like appendages that seemed to move independently as it rotated through the sky.

The couple watched the strange spectacle for approximately three minutes before it abruptly vanished. "It disappeared almost as quickly as it came," Osborn said - dismissing suggestions that the object was an ordinary kite. "It was very clearly not a kite in its movements," she insisted.

The couple even looked around the area afterward, hoping to figure out what they'd just seen, but found nothing.

Osborn admitted it could have been a drone, though she still couldn't explain its bizarre shape or the strange way it moved through the sky.

Nobody knows exactly what the object was, how big it was, or how close it actually came to the military base. And despite all the UFO speculation, there's no evidence it had anything to do with aliens.

Jellyfish UFOs Are Not New

More than four months before he and journalist George Knapp released their Iraq footage, Jeremy Corbell was describing a jellyfish-shaped object on Joe Rogan's podcast. On the Aug. 31, 2023 episode, Corbell said a "very credible witness" at "a totally restricted facility" had told him its weapons couldn't lock onto something that came through. "If you have like an aerostat or something and it's got this thermal camera and you can lock on and shoot out a tire of an Al-Qaeda truck at 23 miles, they couldn't lock," Corbell told Rogan. "The thing was actively jamming their weapon system."

He then turned to Pantex, the nuclear weapons plant outside Amarillo, Texas, where he said there had been "numerous events" of intrusions. In one, he said, "there was an object that came right between the nuclear missile holding facilities." "It looks more like a jellyfish than it did like a saucer," Corbell said, before it shot off at a 45-degree angle.

In January 2024, Corbell and Knapp, who host the Weaponized podcast together, released what they called the raw footage: about 30 seconds of thermal video, shot from an aerostat, of a dark, tentacled object drifting over a US joint operations base in Iraq. Corbell said the object "displayed transmedium capability" and had been "officially designated by the United States intelligence agencies as a UAP." According to the pair, it dropped into a body of water, stayed under for about 17 minutes, then came back out and shot off at high speed. On their show, they said the Pantex object had been filmed on night vision and thermal, and described it as a dome about 8 to 10 feet wide with tentacle-like appendages hanging down.

Today we release the RAW footage of a military filmed UAP incursion within a United States joint operations base. This UAP of unknown origin displayed transmedium capability - and has been officially designated by the United States intelligence agencies as a UAP (Unidentified... pic.twitter.com/gomB8N2eI2

— Jeremy Kenyon Lockyer Corbell (@JeremyCorbell) January 9, 2024

Asked about the video, Pentagon spokeswoman Sue Gough told NewsNation the Department of Defense does not "comment on the authenticity of alleged DOD material that may have been leaked."

Michael Cincoski, a former Marine who worked as an intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance tactical controller at the base, told the outlet that troops there called the object the "spaghetti monster," not the jellyfish, and that it was spotted at the end of 2017. He said the full video shows it getting smaller until it drifts out of view, not plunging into the water or shooting into the sky. It became, he said, "the ghost story of the base."

In June, CNN reported that the pilot of a US F-15 shot down over Iran in April had told intelligence officials he saw Iranian drones flying in a jellyfish formation before he ejected: "Multiple drones interconnected and moving as one with smaller drones below the bigger drones like legs. Real alien sh*t," as one source relayed his account, as we reported. Intelligence officials disagreed over whether the pilot, who was concussed, could recount clearly what he saw.

The Pentagon's fourth batch of UAP records, released July 10, included 2020 infrared footage from the Atlantic Ocean of a dark object about 12 to 15 feet tall that drew immediate comparisons to the Iraq jellyfish, as we reported. The weapons systems officer who filed the debrief described it as "a darker, maroonish color" and wrote that "Structurally, it appeared as a large, somewhat deformed balloon."

The same release included a Department of Energy incident report from Pantex. In September 2015, ground surveillance radar picked up an object over the plant, gates into its security areas were locked, and a security lieutenant and officer who followed it on the ground described a silent "diamond" type shape about 4 feet tall, rounder at the top, with no propulsion they could see. Statements and video went to the FBI, and the video was sent to Sandia National Laboratories for further study, according to the report.

items.title: America's Beer Slump Summed Up In One Chart
items.content_text:
America's Beer Slump Summed Up In One Chart

Bank of America analysts spot a sobering milestone for America's beer industry: shipments are on track to fall below 1980 levels this year as stretched household budgets collide with changing drinking habits. The explosion of GLP-1 drug demand, cannabis products, and growing health concerns about booze are adding pressure on demand. 

BofA consumer staples analysts led by Peter Galbo outlined three key industry takeaways in a Tuesday note following their attendance at the annual Beer Insights Seminar, hosted by Beer Marketer's Insights (BMI) in New York City:

  1. STZ/Hispanic consumer remains top of mind following a mixed weekend for immigration policy. STZ traded higher today, suggesting investors interpreted the developments favorably, while Nicholas Fink reiterated that the Hispanic consumer remains a long-term tailwind for the portfolio. 
  2. Growth continues to shift beyond traditional beer and into RTDs, which continue to see strong growth, while the emerging "ade" segment could represent the next meaningful growth pocket.
  3. Optimism around NA beer remains high, with Athletic Brewing seeing a path for the category to ultimately reach ~20% of total beer.

Shifting focus to the broader industry, Galbo said US beer shipments fell 3.9% through September. He cited data from BMI that showed if this trajectory holds, this would send annual shipments to 176 million barrels, below the 178 million shipped in 1980. 

Galbo said BMI's data show a combination of financial pressure and changing drinking habits. Higher prices, inflation, and weaker consumer sentiment are weighing on demand, while ready-to-drink cocktails are capturing beer demand. He pointed out that hemp-derived THC beverages, GLP-1 drugs and increasingly negative sentiment toward alcohol are adding further headwinds.

Within the industry, the pressure is uneven. Constellation Brands and AB InBev gained volume share, while Molson Coors and Boston Beer lost the most. Growth remains concentrated in canned cocktails and select nonalcoholic beer brands.

"Finally, the industry is undergoing a changing of the guard: all five of the largest U.S. beer suppliers have changed or announced changes to CEOs over roughly the past 15 months as companies manage core beer declines and search for growth in adjacencies," the analyst said.

More broadly, Italian spirits group Campari, maker of Aperol, Wild Turkey, SKYY vodka and Grand Marnier, reported an unexpected decline in third-quarter North American sales late last month.

"In North America, we are still growing, just to be clear, but the overall growth trajectory for this year is being impacted by the US," CEO Simon Hunt told analysts.

The shift in consumer habits away from alcohol comes as we recently cited a report that found daily marijuana use in the US has surpassed daily alcohol consumption among adults.

items.title: Trump Wins Major Ruling In Defamation Lawsuit Against BBC
items.content_text:
Trump Wins Major Ruling In Defamation Lawsuit Against BBC

Authored by Jonathan Turley via Jonathan Turley,

President Donald Trump's lawsuit against the BBC for defamation just received a green light from a federal judge to go forward to trial. Judge Jeffrey Kuntz (S.D. Fla.) ruled in Trump v. BBC that the media outlet must stand trial for splicing together lines from Trump's January 6th speech to make it seem more violence-inducing before the riot at the Capitol. Judge Kuntz, however, rejected a claim under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. The biggest challenge for the court may be whether it can seat jurors who can overcome the case's underlying political elements.

Judge Kuntz, a Trump nominee, notes prior cases brought by the President that federal courts dismissed as not actionable. See Trump v. CNN (S.D. Fla. 2023), aff'd (11th Cir. 2025); Trump v. Dow Jones & Co., Inc. (S.D. Fla. 2026). As a torts professor, I was critical of some past filings by the President that pursued overbroad or flawed defamation claims.

BBC was different. It involved an act that is anathema to ethical journalists - cutting lines from different parts of a tape and then joining them as if they were stated together. Even BBC's own journalists admitted that what they did in the segment violated the most basic ethical standards taught in journalism schools.

The case stems from a documentary denounced as a BBC "hit piece" that aired just a week before the 2024 election, on October 28, 2024. Titled "Trump: A Second Chance," BBC showed a twelve-second segment from Trump's January 6, 2021 speech:

We're going to walk down to the Capitol and I'll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell and if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore.

Those two lines actually were stated fifty-five minutes apart. Moreover, Trump also expressly told his followers to go to the Hill "peacefully" to let their voices be heard - words routinely edited out by many in the media and, most notoriously, by the Democratic J6 Committee,

However, the BBC effectively created a new statement by splicing together two lines. What was actually said was very different from what aired. First, Trump declared:

Now it is up to Congress to confront this egregious assault on our democracy. And after this, we're going to walk down and I'll be there with you. We're going to walk down, we're going to walk down. Anyone you want but I think right here, we're going to walk down to the Capitol and we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them.

Fifty-five minutes later, Trump stated:

[B]ut I said 'Something's wrong here, Something's really wrong, can't have happened.' And we fight, we fight like hell, and if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore.

Notably, less than a minute later, Trump told his supporters to remain peaceful:

I know that everyone here will soon be marching over to the Capitol building to peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard[.]

Judge Jeffrey Kuntz found that the BBC not only recognized its violation of journalistic ethics but actively sought to guarantee that the misleading segment would be heard before the election in states such as Florida.

This decision is notable because Trump must meet a higher standard under Supreme Court precedent. Under New York Times v. Sullivan, the Supreme Court crafted the actual malice standard that required public officials to shoulder the higher burden of proving defamation. Under that standard, an official would have to show either actual knowledge of its falsity or a reckless disregard of the truth. That standard was later extended to public figures.

The court found sufficient evidence of actual malice at BBC:

"For purposes of the defamation test, ill-will is different from actual malice. An intention to portray a public figure in a negative light, even when motivated by ill-will or evil intent, is not sufficient to show actual malice unless the publisher intended to inflict harm through knowing or reckless falsehood. However, ill-will or motive, when combined with other evidence, may be taken into account for actual malice....

Here, Trump alleges that BBC has a history of unfair or improper coverage toward him. In addition to the Documentary itself, Trump highlights the Prescott Memorandum, a 2022 BBC Newsnight episode, and the "2024 BBC News Shooting Hoax." As an important reminder, the state of mind required for actual malice must be "brought home" to the person in the BBC's organization responsible for the publication of the Documentary. This principle is relevant as it relates to the 2022 Newsnight episode and the 2024 "Shooting Hoax." Again, Trump has not alleged that either of these incidents involved the creator(s) of the Documentary. That said, these incidents are not merely portrayal in a negative light, but examples of BBC playing fast and loose with the factual accuracy of their media content. With respect to the Newsnight episode, the BBC seemingly did not care about the falsity of the portrayal until the later Documentary became an issue. Such examples can be said to be probative of BBC's state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC's non-action toward false statements about Trump.

Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump. BBC asks the Court to put on blinders and treat the Panorama team as if they were blocked off from the rest of the organization, ignorant of everything else going on at BBC. At this procedural stage [i.e., a motion to dismiss, where plaintiff must merely plausibly allege facts that could lead to liability, rather than proving them -EV], the Court simply cannot ignore the circumstantial evidence presented. To do so would make it extremely difficult to ever prove a defendant's subjective state of mind in any defamation case....

Trump alleged that BBC's editing of the speech was an "intentional and malicious effort to falsely and deceptively portray President Trump as having called for violence." In support, Trump alleges that it "would have been impossible for BBC's journalists and producers to splice together two distinct parts of the [s]peech from nearly fifty-five minutes apart unless they were acting intentionally." On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice. BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.

Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech. BBC also had the entire speech available to them for nearly three years by the time of the Documentary."

Judge Kuntz adds an interesting twist to the record. The BBC Chairman previously issued an apology:

"The way the speech was edited in the documentary gave a misleading impression of what you said. The editing unintentionally created the impression of a single continuous section of your speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech. This gave the mistaken impression that you had made a direct call for violent action. That was an editorial error and it should not have happened."

However, the court notes that "BBC now appears to disagree with the apology issued by the Chairman:

"BBC's Chairman admitted that the documentary gave a misleading and mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action. Strangely enough, BBC strays from that position in the Motion to Dismiss, referring to statements made by January 6 defendants as evidence that the speech may be interpreted as a call to violent action. But BBC's own Chairman acknowledged the editing was misleading in his letter to Trump...."

The court also notes:

"BBC then argues that allegations that BBC omitted portions of Trump's speech are also insufficient to establish actual malice. Alterations of quotes that "materially alter" the meaning of Trump's statements could support a finding of actual malice.... BBC did not just alter the quote but created a new quote by splicing two statements together and passing them off as a single continuous sentence. To the extent that there was no material alteration to the meaning of Trump's speech, that simply cannot be the case. The Chairman's letter makes it very clear that BBC acknowledges there was a material change of meaning when they edited the speech to create a single continuous segment that did not exist.

BBC then argues that the apology "militates against a finding of actual malice." ... Today, retractions can be issued near instantaneously for online publications thanks to the internet. The Court acknowledges that media entities, like The Washington Post, or BBC, are not perfect, and make mistakes. However, it cannot be said that a retraction the next day is in the same ballpark as a retraction over a year later, and only after being threatened with legal action. The temporal distance here makes the retraction a weak indicator as to BBC's state of mind at the time of publication.

Further weakening BBC's argument, BBC was aware that such editing created a false impression as early as 2022. Former Acting White House Chief of Staff Mick Mulvaney, in relation to the 2022 Newsnight episode, stated on-air: "Your video actually spliced together the presentation.... [Y]our video makes it look like those two things came together." As BBC's own Clive Coleman stated "[t]he first lesson ... you're taught as a broadcast journalist is that you do not joint two bits of footage together from different times in a way that will make the audience think that it is one piece of footage." Considering these facts, BBC's ultimate retraction in 2025 reads less like a readiness to retract, and more like a reluctance to retract."

While the Court acknowledges that some of the evidence from decisions made after the segment aired might not directly bear on the state of mind at the time of publication, it finds that "Trump's allegations regarding BBC's departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence." The key question is whether Trump is allowed a trial to prove such allegations:

"Of course, all of this does not prove BBC acted with actual malice. But it does make it plausible. And Trump need only allege facts sufficient to give rise to a reasonable inference that the BBC edited and published the Documentary 'with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.' Trump has done so here..."

It is a comprehensive and informative opinion. While I have criticized some past lawsuits, I believe the court is right to set this case for trial.

Jonathan Turley is the best-selling author of "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution." He teaches torts and defamation. For full disclosure, Turley previously worked as the BBC's legal analyst.

Here is the opinion: Trump v. BBC

America's Most Dangerous City Sees Stunning 931% Surge In Millionaire Homeowners

Apparently, even the most dangerous big cities can attract millionaires.

Memphis, Tennessee, the Southern city infamous for its violent crime problem, has experienced an explosion in wealthy homeowners, according to newly released housing data.

Research released by RentCafe showed that the number of Memphis-area homeowner households earning at least $1 million annually surged 931% between 2020 and 2024.

That's a jump from just 52 households to 536 in four years.

The increase puts Memphis among the nation's 20 fastest-growing metropolitan areas for millionaire-income homeowners, trailing only Knoxville within Tennessee.

Here's where things get interesting...

Memphis has consistently ranked among America's most violent major cities, recording approximately 1,849 violent crimes per 100,000 residents in 2025.

The situation became so dire that President Donald Trump announced a federal crackdown last year, describing conditions as "dire in one of our Nation's most historic cities."

"The city of Memphis, Tennessee, is suffering from tremendous levels of violent crime that have overwhelmed its local government's ability to respond effectively. This situation has become dire in one of our Nation's most historic cities," the White House said in a statement at the time.

Crime has been easing, though. Nine of the 10 offenses the Council on Criminal Justice tracks were lower in Memphis in 2025 than in 2024, with homicide down 24%, robbery down 30% and carjackings down 48%.

Yet while the city's reputation has been dominated by shootings, robberies and federal intervention, a very different story has been unfolding in its housing market.

However, there's an important catch buried in these numbers. RentCafe's definition of millionaire homeowners refers to households earning at least $1 million annually, not necessarily those with seven-figure net worths. Meanwhile, institutional investors have been snapping up Memphis properties at an extraordinary pace, accounting for 14.8% of home purchases across the metropolitan area during the first quarter of 2026, more than double the national average of 6.6%, according to the Memphis Business Journal. That was second only to Mobile, Ala., at 15%, and on far greater volume: 525 investor purchases in Memphis against 63 in Mobile, the Journal reported. The buying spree continued into the first half of 2026, with investors purchasing roughly one in five Memphis-area homes sold at a median price of just $126,500, according to Realtor.com.

items.title: Members Of Kennedy Family Sue To Block Construction Of Trump's Triumphal Arch
items.content_text:
Members Of Kennedy Family Sue To Block Construction Of Trump's Triumphal Arch

Authored by Aldgra Fredly via The Epoch Times,

Nine Kennedy family members sued on Nov. 10 to block President Donald Trump's planned construction of a triumphal arch in the nation's capital, saying it would cast shadows over their relatives' graves at Arlington National Cemetery.

Trump's White House unveiled plans to build a 250-foot arch in Memorial Circle on Columbia Island, at the western end of Arlington Memorial Bridge. It would feature a mezzanine at 166 feet, a 24-foot observation deck, and a 60-foot Lady Liberty statue on top.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan had temporarily blocked construction of the arch on Nov. 5, just hours after the National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in an 8-4 vote.

The ruling followed lawsuits filed by a group of Vietnam War veterans, the District of Columbia, and the state of Virginia. The Board of Arlington County, Virginia, also filed a separate suit to block the project.

The nine members of the Kennedy family have now joined the legal challenge. In a Nov. 10 court filing, the family said the arch would damage "historically significant sightlines" to their relatives' memorials at Arlington National Cemetery and the memorials honoring fallen American heroes.

The plaintiffs included seven children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy (RFK) and Ethel Kennedy and a grandchild, as well as the son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy, the youngest brother of former President John F. Kennedy (JFK) and RFK. The three are buried in Arlington Cemetery, near the grave of JFK, according to the suit.

"A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy, two of RFK's 11 children, said in a statement announcing the suit on behalf of the family members.

The Kennedy family argued that the administration had not obtained congressional approval required to start commemorative construction works in the nation's capital.

The Epoch Times reached out to the White House for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

Trump said on Sept. 20 that the proposed arch would also serve as a military facility capable of storing and deploying drones and positioning snipers, citing a request from the U.S. military for national security purposes.

The Arlington County Board in its Oct. 8 lawsuit argued that using the arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers would increase the risk of accidents, given its proximity to commuters and tourists.

A spokesperson for the Interior Department told The Epoch Times at the time that the department "continues to follow all laws and regulations" without elaborating further.

Chutkan issued a restraining order on Nov. 5, barring the administration for 14 days from carrying out "any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity at or near Memorial Circle" related to the triumphal arch.

Alina Habba, the former Trump lawyer and New Jersey US attorney who now goes by Alina Habba Mildon, has been fired from the general counsel job that guaranteed her more than $50 million over four years, cut loose by a company set up by the daughter of a billionaire banker President Trump pardoned in January. items.title: Ron Paul: Will Republicans Learn Their Lesson From The 'Disastrous' Midterms?

Ron Paul: Will Republicans Learn Their Lesson From The 'Disastrous' Midterms?

Authored by Ron Paul via Ron Paul Institute,

Politicians break campaign promises with hardly any hesitation and usually they get away with it. Americans have come to put up with broken promises for so long, they hardly even seem to notice. Last week, however, voters noticed. They showed the Republican party just how angry they were over President Trump's decision to attack Iran and how angry they were with Congress for abandoning its Constitutional authority over matters of war and peace.

The results were dramatic. Voters even turned Texas blue, as Democrats took firm control of both the House and Senate.

As President Trump's promise of a quick war and a quick victory rapidly faded, the costs of the unnecessary and illegal attack thousands of miles away soon began to hit Americans hard. The predictable closure of the Hormuz Strait sent fuel costs through the roof, fanning the fires of inflation which hit everything transported by road, rail, or air.

For months the polls were clear: Americans' top three concerns were high fuel prices, inflation, and the Iran war. All were related yet Republicans ignored voter concerns. Last Tuesday, voters had the final say.

The peace candidate usually wins, and President Trump promised repeatedly on the campaign trail that not only would he not start wars, but he would end existing conflicts. But we've heard it all before. George W. Bush was elected promising a "more humble" foreign policy. After eight years of Bush's Middle East wars, Obama was elected as the "new" peace candidate. However soon the "Saddam must go" of the Bush era became "Assad must go" and "Gaddafi must go" in the Obama era. Trump was elected after Biden took us to the brink of war with Russia over Ukraine. He promised that this time he would be the real peace candidate. We got war on Iran instead - a war that we did not win and cannot win.

Has the Republican party gotten the message? Have they learned the lesson voters can deliver when they finally have had enough of being lied to?

Neocons are seeing the voter rebuke of Trump as an opportunity to return the Republican party to the Bush era. Yes, prices and inflation are a problem, they argue, but that has nothing to do with the Iran war.

Nobody is buying that.

Vice President Vance laid out clearly why Republicans lost in the midterms: the war, inflation, rejection of America first, and our unhealthy relationship with Israel. Bush-era neocons like Marc Thiessen were furious, accusing Vance of being "disloyal" to the President.

Does Vance really mean what he said, or is it just another example of politicians promising what they think voters want to hear?

It seems a Republican Party that drummed out Thomas Massie over his opposition to the "Big Beautiful Bill," who warned about the dangers of putting foreign countries before our own, and who demanded an end to all foreign aid is not a Republican Party that Americans are interested in.

The pain will continue until the Party finally rids itself of the neocons and warmongers and returns to its roots as exemplified in the past by the late Sen. Robert Taft and in the present by Massie, Marjorie Taylor Greene, Joe Kent, Tucker Carlson, and many others who genuinely care about peace and liberty.

items.title: "Lots Of Distressing And Borderline Disturbing Reports"
items.content_text:
"Lots Of Distressing And Borderline Disturbing Reports"

By Michael Every of Rabobank

As has been the norm in 2026 to date, there are lots of distressing and borderline disturbing reports this morning and very little sign of progress where it’s needed. For once these surprises don’t all cluster in the messy world of geopolitics – and one is right in the middle of inflation and monetary policy.

Yesterday’s US CPI print came in hotter than expected at 0.4% m-o-m headline vs. a consensus of 0.3% and 0.3% core vs. a 0.2% market view. To put it in the words of the usually dovish Fed voter Goolsbee, “It’s another distressing report, borderline disturbing. We’ve been hoping to get progress.” Instead, we saw an acceleration in grocery and food inflation, persistent housing/shelter price pressure, and a delayed pass-through from earlier energy shocks feeding into medical care, household furnishings, and other daily expenses.

The reaction in US 2-year yields was dramatic - they jumped 19bps while 10-year yields rose 14bps to briefly go back above 5% again; today, we have a Bloomberg story talking about the possibility of a 50bps hike from the Fed! 

Of course, that US yield spike came just after everyone rushed back into Treasuries after the AI and bullish oil trades hit an air pocket with last week’s US election on the view that the former is likely to be slowed down and that we are closer to peace than war in the Middle East on the back of the recent Democrat Blue Tsunami. Now imagine if either of those were not the case.

On AI, nobody knows what will happen next. However, as headlines along the lines of the old Bond film ‘The Spy Who Loved Me’ swirl around the Nvidia CEO, the Financial Times headline today is that Anthropic’s bankers are preparing to increase its IPO valuation to $1.5 trillion. 

On the geopolitical front, Trump just said the US will continue with a full sea and land economic blockade of Iran and that new strikes are “highly unlikely.” However, the Jerusalem Post cites diplomatic sources that Qatar’s prime minister told G7 foreign ministers Doha had secured “at least two weeks” to pursue an understanding between D.C. and Tehran before US escalation. Presuming this was achieved last weekend, where other reports suggest the US was moments away from striking, that means we could still be looking at more fighting by mid- to end-November, at which time a third US aircraft carrier will be in the region. That’s a distressing report.

That is, unless an agreement can be reached: yet the US Secretary of State and Iranian officials insist the other side is intractable. Tehran also just demonstrated to its media the scale of its remaining underground missile city facilities, as western intelligence reports point to the ability to produce up to 50 missiles a month despite the US blockade. 

Other logistical movements point to a high risk of looming conflict. The US just relocated 10 refuelling planes from a second UK airbase for fear of Iranian retaliation, an indictment of Western security – but retaliation for what if no attacks are planned? 

And recall the war is on more than one front. Syrian officials have denied reports that thousands of its troops have been deployed to aid Saudi forces against the Houthis in Yemen, stating they are only there for “training, expertise exchange and military consultations.” A useful coincidence as Syria considers joining the Mecca Pact, under which Egyptian and Pakistani troops are already present in Saudi alongside French and British fighter jets.

Meanwhile, in Abu Dhabi, Russia, Ukraine, and the US held talks about a “final end” to the war and a “new European security architecture.” On the former, Zelenskyy the initial discussions as “constructive and fairly substantive,” but that Putin lives in “a different reality.” On the latter, it’s notable Europe wasn’t present. When changes to one’s home’s architecture are planned you usually get a say(!) – but not the case when much of the architecture is (for now) provided by others. 

In a best-case scenario, this may lead to a frozen conflict between Russia and Ukraine. In the worst-case scenarios, the talks collapse and we go back to escalation; or, less likely, fears are the US might agree with Russian demands for a roll-back of NATO and a seat at Europe’s table as the price for peace. That’s a stark binary with potentially equally stark impact on Europe across different dimensions. It’s borderline disturbing to have to talk about borders and lines (on maps and screens) like that.

Linking this Great Power zeitgeist back to markets, Bloomberg today notes that Russia has effectively abandoned attempts to replace the dollar with CNY due to US secondary sanctions, the yuan's share in payments for Russian exports halving to 22%, and Russia now receiving RUB for 69% of its exports to Asia. That leaves Russian businesses with slower, more expensive, less predictable, and more complex payment routes and shows some of the power the US can bring to bear in the financial space even as its shortfalls in terms of military industries are equally evident.

On the same zeitgeist, Canadian PM Carney publicly stated that regarding China: “In terms of the security risks for our partnership, they’re much, much, much less than the security risks, for example, of the United States.” Trumpian rhetoric and Carney’s talk of a US invasion aside(!), Canada and the US are still NATO allies and members of NORAD. The PM’s rhetoric may be a negotiating position over tariffs - but it remains to be seen if the new Blue US Congress is prepared to lower those vs. Canada if Ottawa is at the same time determined to integrate its economy more closely with China’s. 

It’s also notable that the Dutch candidate to replace ECB President Lagarde, Klaas Knot, gave an interview to the Financial Times in which he stated, “If circumstances require it, we will not hesitate to take action.” He wasn’t referring to 50bps rate hikes due to geopolitically driven inflation but in the opposite direction, where if Europe were to see a future crisis “of a different nature,” he “would not rule out developing another, more tailored instrument.” Yet given potential crises could emerge from the absence of black, sticky, liquid products rather than digital financial liquidity, is there a tacit implication that “Whatever it takes” might need to become “Wherever it takes us”? 

If so, is that reassuring, a distressing report, or borderline disturbing?

Oil Jumps Amid Fresh Tanker Attack; Iran Insists Nuclear Materal Won't Leave Its Soil

Update(10:45ET): Several bits of negative news out of Iran and the Strait of Hormuz have served to push oil prices higher Wednesday morning. Yet another tanker has been struck by a sea mine in the strait, adding to what's become a daily and weekly tally. The attacks have come so frequently at this point that international maritime monitors are struggling to keep up with fresh data. According to the latest:

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says that a tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine. Iran’s state media reports the tanker was traveling through an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway.

The British military said a tanker was involved in an incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, or UKMTO, did not identify the tanker, and further details of the incident were not immediately available.

Additionally, as detailed below, Iran has firmly rejected prior reports that it is negotiating the nuclear file with Washington. Top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei has rejected the prospect of transferring enriched uranium out of the country as part of any future deal to end the war.

Spike in crude amid a steady climb this week:

* * *

Contradicting earlier Gulf-sourced reports from this week, top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei has rejected the prospect of transferring enriched uranium out of the country as part of any deal with the US.

He weighed in during an interview with Lebanon's Al Mayadeen TV, wherein Rezaei again slammed the door shut on Iran sending its stockpile of 60% enriched uranium to a third country.

Rezaei, who serves as the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), stressed that the Islamic Republic would not "remove a single atom of enriched nuclear material" and that Russia is aware of Tehran’s position.

Russia had earlier in the conflict offered to receive and store the highly enriched uranium - an overture which presumably still stands, but which Tehran is for now also rejecting.

The fresh statements come after Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, and amid what appears to be Moscow's stepped up diplomatic involvement in seeking to resolve the crisis in the region.

According a Al Jazeera, "While Iran has repeatedly rejected the transfer of its uranium, it has not ruled out diluting the uranium to a lower enrichment level under international supervision."

Additionally in the comments, Rezaei characterized some recent reporting coming out the West on the status of negotiations as fake:

His comments come as reports swirl over a potential meeting between him and US Vice President JD Vance to negotiate a deal that reopens the Strait of Hormuz and ends the war against Iran, now in its ninth month.

Al Mayadeen quoted Rezaei as saying that there were no talks being held between Tehran and Washington, dismissing reports of a recent meeting in Qatar as “pure lies” meant to drive down oil prices which have risen around the world due to instability in the Middle East sparked by the war.

That's precisely the process that seems to have been playing out at the opening of this week. Negotiation 'optimism' gets floated chiefly in Gulf news sources, only to hours later be batted down as false by the Iranian side.

Rezaei has stressed that the US was "manufacturing fake news" about talks.

Iran has still insisted its seven conditions must be met, and that it won't negotiate the nuclear file until after the war is ended (and after these seven are fulfilled). As it stands, the seven are:

1. An end to the war on all fronts, including Lebanon

2. Lifting the US naval blockade of Iran

3. Releasing Iran's frozen assets

4. Lifting Iran sanctions imposed after the Islamabad Agreement

5. Withdrawal of US forces from the geography around Iran

6. Iranian oil sales to be exempted from sanctions

7. Recognition of the maritime corridor agreed upon by Iran and Oman. There will be no nuclear discussions until these conditions are met. 

Middle East regional journalist and pundit Sharmine Narwani observes, "The Strait of Hormoz will not reopen until the US accepts and executes these terms, verifiably. Iran will no longer be flexible - that opportunity was forever lost once the US and Israel launched a war of aggression."

Meanwhile, Professor Robert Pape says that if Tehran has decided to build a bomb, there's basically nothing the US can do about it at this point.

Interestingly, war reparations are not mentioned in the above list, and this point was always seen as the most unrealistic for Washington to ever agree to.

However, Rubio this week cited war reparations as precisely the non-starter Tehran is still apparently sticking to, which he says shows Tehran is not yet serious about achieving a lasting peace deal.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and special envoy to the talks (alongside Steve Witkoff), said after the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended.

Precise numbers of POWs have yet to be given, but Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky also confirmed it.

"We have agreed on a new, large-scale prisoner exchange," Medinsky told reporters, noting that the "concrete" details of the exchange would be forthcoming.

"Together with the American side, we exchanged our views ​on this; on some points we reached a common ​understanding, whilst on ‌others we did not. And this discussion will, of course, continue. The world needs a new, modern, updated security system – one that ‌is fair and does not disadvantage any particular countries," Medinsky ‌said as cited in European media. And most significantly:

Russian Official Ushakov says "the possibility of holding a bilateral meeting between Russian President Putin and US President Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit is currently being discussed and studied."

And...

Russia's Medinsky says they see no possibility of territorial exchanges with Ukraine, Tass reports.

Wishing to keep up the momentum in dialogue, Russian President Putin is expected to meet US envoys Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday morning, who are flying to Moscow.

Kushner proclaims that "openings and opportunities" have been presented...

Washington's peace efforts have so far have failed to result in a peace breakthrough, and at the same time Ukraine's Zelensky has been complaining that the Europeans must be at the table 'every step of the way'.

However, the BBC on Tuesday cited US officials to say that Ukraine and Russia have privately shown "a little bit of flexibility" over disputed territory.

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," an official remarked on the trilateral talks process. Zelensky is under pressure from the Trump administration to give up territory, and to also finally hold elections, but he also has a hardline nationalist base to not concede or compromise in any significant way.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO Order Book Reportedly Booms But Graveyard Of 'Oversubscribed Deals' Signals Warning
items.content_text:
Anthropic's IPO Order Book Reportedly Booms But Graveyard Of 'Oversubscribed Deals' Signals Warning

Summary:

  • Bloomberg Says Anthropic IPO "Multiple Times" Oversubscribed 
  • Managing partner in Peter Thiel's family office Warns Anthropic IPO underperformance Could Pop AI 
  • Anthropic Bankers Push For Higher IPO Valuation 

Anthropic IPO Oversubscribed But What Happens Next?

Anthropic's IPO roadshow is underway, and reports that the lead bankers on the deal want to boost its valuation before trading starts next Thursday hit the headlines earlier today.

Adding to those developments, Bloomberg cites sources saying Anthropic's IPO has "drawn multiple times the orders for the shares available," signaling strong demand.

The Claude chatbot maker revealed in a Tuesday S-1 filing that it's seeking to raise as much as $90.4 billion through the IPO and a private placement. But bankers on the deal say the offering of 825 million shares, currently marketed at $70 to $78 each under the ticker ANT, could price above that range, pushing its fully diluted valuation beyond the roughly $1.4 trillion currently targeted.

In fact, bankers are pushing for total fundraising well above $100 billion, likely reflecting strong demand. But a review of past IPOs, follow-on offerings and debt deals shows that oversubscription doesn't necessarily translate into higher prices down the road.

For instance, Klarna and StubHub had heavily oversubscribed IPOs, yet both traded below their offering prices. 

More recently, Cerebras, SpaceX and Jersey Mike's IPOs were roughly 20 times, four times and 10 times subscribed, respectively. Follow-on offerings from Alphabet, Intel, Meta and Strive also attracted strong demand, yet most of these stocks now trade below their offering prices, with SpaceX and Strive the exceptions.

Recent debt offerings from Oracle, SpaceX, Paramount Skydance and Amazon were also oversubscribed, yet those bonds traded at higher yields.

The takeaway is that bullish headlines about an oversubscribed deal are no guarantee of returns, and with cracks forming in the AI bubble and Democrats threatening nationwide data center moratoriums, the investment outlook for AI stocks looks shaky. 

As for Anthropic, we return to this morning's Bloomberg TV interview with Jack Selby, who runs venture capital firm Copper Sky and is a managing partner at Peter Thiel's family office. He warned that the worst outcome for the AI bubble would be an underperforming Anthropic IPO.

Anthropic Bankers Push For Higher IPO Valuation Amid Warnings That Weak Debut Could Prick AI Bubble

Nasdaq futures rallied Wednesday morning after CoreWeave's earnings showed strong sales growth, lifting Taiwanese and Korean equities overnight. Improving sentiment around the AI trade is emerging after last week's Democratic sweep sparked crisis fears about potential data center moratoriums.

Nadsaq Futs

Ahead of Anthropic's mega IPO, expected next Thursday, sentiment toward the AI trade must improve. An underperforming IPO could mark the top of the AI bubble, according to Jack Selby, who runs the venture capital firm Copper Sky and managing partner in Peter Thiel's family office, in an interview with Bloomberg TV earlier today.

UBS Hyperscalers

Morgan Stanley Neocloud Basket

Anthropic's IPO roadshow began Tuesday as the "fair value" of what could be the biggest IPO ever slid from $2 trillion to $1.5 trillion, then to $1.2 trillion. Dario's chatbot company filed an amended S-1 yesterday revealing plans to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each under the ticker ANT, with pricing set for next Wednesday night and trading set to begin on Thursday.

And now, a new report from The Financial Times says that bankers on the IPO want to boost Anthropic's valuation to north of $1.5 trillion.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which are leading the IPO, expect pricing could exceed the $70-to-$78 range because of strong demand. 

The S-1 showed that Anthropic aims to raise as much as $64 billion through the public offering, with an overallotment option adding almost $10 billion. Google, Nvidia and Microsoft have separately committed a combined $26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price. Higher pricing could push total fundraising well above $100 billion, exceeding SpaceX's offering from early summer. 

"Three of the company's backers said Anthropic was now focused on raising as much as possible via the listing to support its heavy spending on computing power, rather than maximizing its valuation," the FT reported.

Morningstar analysts put the estimated fair equity value at $1.7 trillion, while Hyperliquid's pre-IPO Anthropic contract implies a valuation of around $1.8 trillion on Wednesday morning.

Returning to Selby's interview with Bloomberg earlier this morning, he warned:

 "An underperforming Anthropic IPO has to be a very prominent player in what will be a pretty massive correction in the market with respect to AI. If the most anticipated AI company's IPO falls very short of its projected valuation, and just imagine where it's going to go after the lockups expire."

Supporting the market between now and next Thursday is the only thing on the minds of anyone with skin in the AI ecosystem game (so everyone), but as The FT notes, citing 'one major investor', "a weekend is an eternity in this market."

items.title: The Cruel Irony Of Veterans Day
items.content_text:
The Cruel Irony Of Veterans Day

Authored by Connor O'Keeffe via The Mises Institute,

Today is Veterans Day. It's a day when politicians like to give speeches praising the extraordinary courage and selflessness of America's veterans and active-duty military personnel.

It's also a day when American military history is often treated like a vague, homogeneous blob of sacrifice. But it's worth getting a bit more specific.

We celebrate on November 11 because that's the day, back in 1918, when World War I ended. It was famously the day when the guns fell silent at the eleventh hour on the eleventh day of the eleventh month.

Less famous is the fact that the agreement to stop fighting had been reached around 5 am that day. But the Allied high command rejected their German counterparts' request that everyone stop firing as quickly as orders could be circulated, opting instead to wait until the more poetic time of 11 am. And, in those last few hours, 2,738 soldiers would lose their lives - including an American private who was shot and killed at 10:59 am, seconds before both sides were officially ordered to cease firing.

However, the tragedy of those last few hours of unnecessary fighting was immediately overtaken by an overwhelming sense of relief. The world had never seen death and destruction at a scale even close to what had just consumed Europe. The military and civilian deaths are estimated to fall somewhere in the range of 15 to 22 million.

As we know now, the war was, unfortunately, only the opening phase of a three-decade-long catastrophe that saw Europe collapse into revolutionary violence, regions like the Middle East torn into territorial disputes that are still ongoing, and the world descend into a second, even larger global war. This period was so destructive and cost humanity so much that now, almost a century later, we're still struggling to fully understand it.

But no one knew that all of that lay ahead 108 years ago today, when the fighting stopped. Still, the day was less a rowdy celebration and more, again, grounded in a sense of relief that the horror in the trenches and the suffering everywhere else the war touched were finally over.

And a year later, when President Wilson proclaimed the anniversary as an American holiday - then called Armistice Day - the day still carried a somber sense of remembrance for those who had died, reflection on the horrors they had gone through, and, above all, urgency for making sure that nothing like it ever happened again.

However, not everyone shared that sense of relief or the weary desire to move fully on from the war. Because several groups had benefited enormously from the institutional changes brought about by the wartime political order.

As Murray Rothbard laid out in his short book War Collectivism (which we're giving away free hard copies of this month), World War I greatly accelerated a trend that had begun in isolated corners of the economy in the preceding decades - known as the Progressive Era. The war helped establish a powerful and durable alliance between the federal government, big business interests, and a class of "progressive" intellectuals who saw the centrally-planned mobilization of resources as an opportunity to move toward their ideal society, one managed by "experts" like them.

Some members of this alliance, such as Rexford Tugwell, explicitly complained that the Armistice had prevented "a great experiment" in government control over production and all parts of society. But the more serious parts of this big business-government-intellectual coalition got to work finding other emergencies to justify not only continuing that kind of wartime federal control, but accelerating it.

That came first in the 1920s with Herbert Hoover's "associationism," which set the stage for the corporate statism of FDR's New Deal in the 1930s. Then World War II, of course, saw an even larger centralization of power in this burgeoning bureaucratic administrative welfare-warfare state. By the time the war ended, the alliance that had initially formed as a "temporary" wartime measure during World War I had fully developed into an identifiable and, importantly, self-interested caste within the American political system.

And that caste has pursued its own interest relentlessly in the decades since. That was somewhat straightforward early on since the Cold War with the Soviet Union seemed to justify all the money, resources, and jobs the federal "national security" apparatus was eating up. But especially since the USSR collapsed in the early 1990s, the bureaucrats, politicians, weapons manufacturers, and related lobbies have had to work hard to find or create enemies and wage perpetual wars to justify all the wealth and power they're awarding themselves, at our expense, every single year.

And Veterans Day has played a part in that effort. In the 1950s, President Eisenhower officially changed Armistice Day to Veterans Day. That was done ostensibly, and somewhat understandably, to include veterans of WWII and Korea in the ceremonies.

But with that shift, the holiday's center of gravity moved from celebrating the end of a particular war to honoring veterans of all wars. And over time, after each major war, the holiday's meaning widened from the initial grateful recognition that a war was over to something of a spotlight for politicians to stress that military service is itself glorious, which has made each next war easier to sell.

And make no mistake, that is precisely what the hawkish politicians and establishment voices we hear today are doing. They are selling unnecessary wars that benefit themselves and their well-connected friends to the population and fighting force that must bear the cost.

And what makes this especially infuriating is what they're exploiting.

There are few human qualities more admirable than the willingness to risk or even sacrifice one's own life to protect others. The instinct that drives someone to put himself in harm's way to defend his family, neighbors, and community is genuinely noble. To be sure, that is not why everyone in the American military has joined up. There are plenty of different reasons soldiers from all different backgrounds have out there, from family history to economic necessity.

But it is still clear, if you take even a passing glance at history, that a willingness to sacrifice one's time, comfort, physical safety, and even life to protect one's community is something that Americans have had in abundance.

The way that willingness to sacrifice has been hijacked by this ever-growing caste of "national security" bureaucrats, hawkish politicians, and weapons companies to wage wars of choice on behalf of their well-connected friends and favorite foreign lobbies is utterly despicable.

Those who died in the final hours of World War I did not need politicians to praise their sacrifice. They needed the men giving the orders and the politicians directing them to stop unnecessarily demanding it.

More than a century later, that is still what we need. And it is the best way to truly honor America's veterans and active-duty soldiers: stop squandering their lives in wars that never needed to be fought.

We publish a variety of perspectives. Nothing written here is to be construed as representing the views of ZeroHedge.

Iran Hawk Bessent Now Lives Behind A Military Gate As Threats Reach 'More Than Advanced Stage'

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved out of his Washington-area home and onto a US military base because of Iranian threats against him, the New York Times reported Tuesday.

A senior administration official told Fox News the threats against Bessent's life had reached "more than an advanced stage," and declined to say when he moved.

BREAKING: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved to a military base after Iranian threats against his life reached "more than an advanced stage," a senior administration official tells Fox News Digital.

The official says the threats prompted Bessent and his family to make... pic.twitter.com/Ei25bRHwRE

— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 11, 2026

The Treasury Department, confirming the move, said Bessent "will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats" and remains committed to the pressure campaign against Tehran.

Bessent has run Operation Economic Outcast since Aug. 24, a campaign he says is meant "to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." Launching it, he declared: "America is no longer managing the Iranian threat. We are ending it."

In September, Treasury sanctioned all of Iran's remaining airlines, with Bessent warning anyone still doing business with them: "You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system." On Nov. 4, a day after Republicans were crushed in midterms widely seen as a referendum on the Iran war, he announced another round, as we reported: "As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us."

Last week, as we noted, MEMRI flagged an Iranian video that calls Bessent "Captain Corruptor" and warns that he "has booked himself a first class ticket to Hell and his ride will soon arrive at his door."

In a memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that "Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" and that "the lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages" in the Middle East and certain other countries.

Bessent and Rubio rode a decoy Air Force One out of Ankara after the NATO summit in July while Trump secretly switched planes. A senior administration official told ABC News that Trump's switch was driven by intelligence that an Iranian terror cell had slipped into Turkey with a shoulder-fired missile.

"Worse than fake news is fake intelligence," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X in response. And as we noted in August, a US official told the Washington Post the Turkey warning was "Israeli-derived, not US-generated, and viewed as low confidence."

Bessent joins a growing list of Trump officials living behind base gates, several of whom moved into military housing last year over threats from the left. Joe Biden was pelted with milk cartons in Dublin, Ireland, as he took cover behind an umbrella. Police wrestled with protesters while he was rushed into his SUV. pic.twitter.com/DCQbCgztYI

Security held up umbrellas over the 83-year-old and former first lady Jill Biden as they were walked to their cars across Trinity's Front Square, while gardaí tackled protesters to the ground and the crowd chanted "Blood, blood, blood on your hands!"

Gardaí told the Jerusalem Post they arrested two men, one in his 50s and one in his 30s, over a public order incident at the college, and that the older man has been charged and is due in court.

Harper Alderson, editor of the student paper the University Times, told RTÉ that gardaí used pepper spray on two protesters, as students surrounded the cars chanting "Genocide Joe" and "Shame on you," and later "guards off our campus." NOW: Irish pro-Pals just tried to get at President Joe Biden as he arrived at a Trinity College in Dublin. The crowd is chanting "blood on your hands". These ghouls will never be appeased. pic.twitter.com/oCluflYoWo

Trinity said the protest in Front Square escalated as the Bidens were leaving the ceremony in the college's Exam Hall, and that the family left without incident.

Inside, Biden had sat in the front row while Hunter, who said he was honored to be in Dublin with his family, spoke about his addiction and a family intervention. Hunter was convicted on federal gun charges and pleaded guilty to tax charges in 2024 before his father pardoned him that December.

Asked about Gaza during the question-and-answer session, Hunter called Israel's bombing campaign "mass murder" and the situation there "absolutely and completely wrong," the Irish Times reported.

items.title: Mo, Mo, & Mo: 3 Charged In Iran-Linked Plot Against British Airbase
items.content_text:
Mo, Mo, & Mo: 3 Charged In Iran-Linked Plot Against British Airbase

A longtime operative of Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hizballah sitting in a New York jail used phone calls to his family in Iraq to pass coded messages to the men who allegedly orchestrated September's plot against RAF Fairford, the British air base that housed US bombers, federal prosecutors say.

An eight-count superseding indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, 32, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian operative of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi national, with terrorism offenses tied to nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States on behalf of Kata'ib Hizballah and the IRGC.

Three days before the vans rolled toward Fairford, on or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi asked his family on a call from jail how "Ali" was doing, according to the Justice Department. Told that "Ali" had been moved to the "International Section," al-Saadi allegedly instructed them to "give him money so we can do it." Prosecutors identify "Ali" as al-Hassani.

"Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

Vans, fuel and fake decals

According to the indictment, al-Hassani and Mohajeri were both in Iran during the plot and worked through a network of contacts in Britain. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani allegedly paid one person to surveil the base's perimeter and received videos of the area.

In September, he allegedly tasked and paid several people to buy vans and barrels of fuel, research large quantities of potassium chloride and other chemical accelerants, and buy metal objects that could serve as shrapnel. At his urging, they had custom decals made so the vans looked like they belonged to a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply company.

On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly sent three vans, some later found to hold barrels of fuel, toward the base, staying in frequent contact with the drivers. At least two of them hit a security roadblock and were turned back, prosecutors say. British police recovered the three white vans in the early hours of Sept. 27 and arrested the occupants.

The US then pulled its B-1 bombers out of Fairford, and British prosecutors last month charged two men under the National Security Act with assisting Iranian intelligence. On Tuesday, as we reported, the Pentagon moved tankers out of a second British base, RAF Mildenhall.

"Our old work"

Al-Saadi was charged in May with planning and promoting about 18 attacks in Europe and attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York; he was arrested abroad on or about May 1. For roughly four months after his arrest, the Justice Department says, there were no further attacks attributable to the three men.

But from jail, prosecutors say, he kept talking about "work," a term he regularly used for terrorist activity. In June and July calls with his mother and sister, he discussed Mohajeri under aliases including "Sayyid Abbas," said he owed him money and asked them to pass messages along. On one call he asked his sister, "What are they doing about all our old work?" She allegedly replied: "it isn't cancelled."

Al-Saadi has pleaded not guilty to the earlier charges, and the Justice Department had already placed him under special administrative measures restricting his contacts to immediate family and lawyers, CNN reported from court records.

"Light it up like a Christmas tree"

The European attacks were claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, which prosecutors call a front for Kata'ib Hizballah. Of the 18 it claimed in spring 2026, seven were in the United Kingdom, more than any other European country, including arsons, explosives and the near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London, one of them a dual US-British citizen.

Prosecutors say a video from about April 6 shows al-Hassani telling Mohajeri, in a room in Iraq with a map of London on a screen, "we need to get focused on London." Six attacks in and around London followed about a week later.

On about April 17, the three men allegedly watched an attack live over FaceTime, projected on a large screen in front of the group's logo, while al-Hassani told the attacker to "light one in your hand" and "throw the fourth one." The next day, on a call with a man attacking a London synagogue, al-Hassani allegedly told him to "light it up like a Christmas tree" before he threw an improvised explosive device at the building.

"The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical - it is very real," said US Attorney Jamie McDonald. The terrorist-organization support and terrorism-financing counts each carry up to 20 years in prison, and the attempted-terrorism and bombing-conspiracy counts up to life.

items.title: UK Trader And "Fake Private Equity Exec" Sentenced Over Fake £154 Million Takeover Bid
items.content_text:
UK Trader And "Fake Private Equity Exec" Sentenced Over Fake £154 Million Takeover Bid

Fake it til you make it? Not always such a great idea...

A British day trader who posed as a private equity executive to orchestrate a fake £154 million ($206 million) takeover bid has received a two-year suspended prison sentence for fraud and forgery, according to a new report from Bloomberg. 

Christopher Woolcott, 44, sought to inflate the share price of Touchstone Exploration after buying shares in London and Toronto. He created multiple false identities, impersonated lawyers and investment executives, and even adopted a Boston accent when meeting the company's CEO at a London hotel in December 2024.

To support the bogus offer, Woolcott used ChatGPT to help forge HSBC proof-of-funds documents and legal correspondence. He also circulated fabricated materials through Discord to lend credibility to the supposed deal.

Bloomberg wrote that Touchstone's management questioned the unusually generous offer, while its lawyers uncovered inconsistencies in the documents.

A London judge called the scheme deliberate and sophisticated but suspended Woolcott's sentence after considering his family circumstances. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority described it as a calculated attempt to manipulate the market.

The scheme began in November 2024, when Woolcott approached Touchstone under the alias Simon Jones of Griffon Partners, proposing an all-cash acquisition at nearly twice the company's market value. He later posed as Jones's business partner, Greg Thomas, during an in-person meeting with Touchstone's CEO.

During sentencing, the judge cited a psychological report in which Woolcott admitted finding it exciting to assume different identities and getting carried away. 

His lawyers argued that financial pressures, tax debts and depression contributed to his actions. The judge also considered his role as the primary breadwinner for his family and father of two young children.

  • 7:00am: MBA Mortgage Applications (week ended Nov. 6), est. n/a, prior 
  • US bond market closed for Veterans Day (SIFMA); stock markets open

Central Bank Speakers

  • No Fed speakers scheduled 

DB's Jim Reid concludes the overnight wrap

Inflation was back on the agenda over the last 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print and hawkish Fed comments drove a major selloff for US Treasuries. In fact, the 2yr Treasury yield (+17.6bps) saw its biggest daily jump since April 2025, surging to 4.74%, and markets even priced a modest chance of a 50bp Fed hike in December. So it was a very rough day for rates, and that in turn put renewed pressure on equities, with the S&P 500 (-0.38%) pulling back as investors priced in faster hikes. To be fair, it wasn’t all bad news, and growing hopes for a resolution in the Middle East pushed Brent crude oil (-1.17%) to its lowest since August, closing at $91.49/bbl. Moreover, positive earnings from CoreWeave have helped equities recover, with S&P 500 futures up +0.65% this morning. But even so, the bigger concern remained that inflation was becoming more persistent and couldn’t just be blamed on a few specific categories.

That US CPI print drove the biggest moves of the day, with the monthly core CPI print for October above consensus at +0.30% (vs. +0.2% expected). Moreover, it was the third consecutive month with core CPI at +0.3%, and if you take those three months together, the annualised pace for core CPI is running at +3.75%. That’s the fastest pace on that measure since April 2024, so it made it increasingly difficult to dismiss this as a blip. Meanwhile, the headline CPI numbers were faster still, with monthly headline CPI at +0.35% (vs. +0.3% expected), with the 3-month annualised pace at +5.72%. Bear in mind there aren’t year-on-year numbers in this report, because last year’s CPI print didn’t happen because of a government shutdown. But overall, there was little respite in the release, with broad-based gains across the consumer basket.

The CPI release got more attention than usual, partly because of comments from Fed Governor Waller a few hours beforehand. He was speaking in London, where he said that “if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings – with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher”, then he thought “a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting”. Indeed, he also said that in those circumstances, a 25bp hike “would put our credibility at risk”. So when the core CPI print was confirmed at 0.3%, that led to mounting speculation about a larger rate hike.

That impact was clear from market pricing, with the amount of hikes for a December up from 21.0bps on Monday to 27.7bps by last night’s close, and 28.5bps this morning. So in other words, a 25bp hike is fully priced in, with futures also pricing in a 14% chance of a larger 50bp move. But it wasn’t just December that was affected, with markets pricing in a more hawkish profile further out the curve as well. Indeed, the rate priced in for the September 2027 meeting was up +22.3bps yesterday, so investors had priced in almost a full additional rate hike to next year’s path. Meanwhile, DB’s own US economists have updated their Fed view, adding a rate hike in January to their profile. So they now expect three more 25bp hikes at the next three meetings (Dec, Jan and March), and you can read their latest update here.

For markets, the clearest impact could be seen in US Treasuries, with yields surging across the curve. In fact, the 2yr Treasury yield (+17.6bps) saw its biggest daily jump since April 2025, the day that Trump paused his Liberation Day tariffs. And those moves extended to longer maturities, with the 10yr yield (+10.8bps) closing back at 4.99%, its highest level in nearly two weeks. Meanwhile, Fed speakers later in the session added to that momentum. For instance, Dallas Fed President Logan said in a speech that “the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases”, and Kansas City Fed President Schmid said that the current policy rate was “fairly accommodative”. Moreover, Chicago Fed President Goolsbee described the print as “borderline disturbing”.

With markets pricing in a more hawkish Fed, that also drove a fresh selloff in US equities, though this did ease a bit as the session went on. Tech stocks underperformed, with a -5.47% drop in Nvidia leading the Nasdaq (-0.74%) and the Mag-7 (-0.83%) to larger declines than the S&P 500 (-0.38%). The broader equity mood was a bit better, however, with almost half of the S&P 500’s constituents higher on the day, and the equal-weighted S&P 500 only down -0.02%. After the close, we then heard from CoreWeave, which delivered a Q3 revenue beat ($3.66bn vs $3.56bn est.) and upgraded its full-year revenue guidance ($13.0-13.3bn vs $12.9bn est.). So that meant its shares rose by over +7% in after-hours trading, easing some of the doubt around the AI cycle. And in turn, that’s boosted optimism more broadly, with Nasdaq 100 futures up +1.40% this morning, and those on the S&P 500 up +0.65%.

As all that was happening, oil prices continued to fall, as hopes continued to rise for some kind of diplomatic resolution in the US-Iran conflict. There wasn’t a single headline driving that, but several comments have pointed away from further strikes, with Trump saying on Monday that “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbors”. So with fears of an escalation receding, that helped Brent crude oil (-1.17%) fall to $91.49/bbl by the close, its lowest since August. And longer-dated futures also moved lower, with the 12-month Brent future (-1.68%) at a two-month low of $77.64/bbl.

Overnight in Asia, that renewed optimism around the AI trade has boosted equities across the region, with the KOSPI (+2.27%) and the Nikkei (+1.33%) posting strong gains. Moreover, the latest data showed South Korea’s unemployment rate unexpectedly falling to a 3-year low of 2.5% in October (vs. 2.6% expected). However, there’s been a weaker performance elsewhere in Asia, with the CSI 300 (+0.02%) and the Shanghai Comp (-0.02%) seeing little movement, whilst the Hang Seng is down -0.83%. Otherwise, the hawkish repricing after the US CPI print has led to a fresh bond selloff in numerous countries. For instance, Japan’s 10yr yields are up +10.3bps this morning to 2.78%, while 10yr yields in Australia (+5.6bps) and New Zealand (+6.8bps) are also higher.

Earlier in Europe, there was a major selloff for sovereign bonds too, although not quite as big as in the US. For instance, yields on 10yr bunds (+5.5bps), OATs (+7.0bps) and BTPs (+7.4bps) all saw a sharp increase. And similarly to the US, investors priced in a more hawkish ECB path for the months ahead as well. For instance, market pricing for a December hike rose from 83% on Monday to 92% by the close. And looking further out, the number of hikes priced in by the June 2027 meeting rose +10.9bps on the day to 58bps. For equities, there was a much more resilient performance in Europe, although that partly reflected a catchup to the rally late in the US session the previous day. So the STOXX 600 (+0.27%) moved higher, alongside the DAX (+0.31%) and the CAC 40 (+0.55%).

Looking at the day ahead now, it’ll be a quieter one, with US bond markets closed for Veterans Day. Central bank speakers will include ECB President Lagarde, and the ECB’s Cipollone, Kazaks and Nagel. Otherwise, data releases include Italian industrial production for September.
