Sure, there are ways in which that’s true. But for God’s sake: Voters in this election emphatically rejected that cliché. Democrats won exurban and rural districts they haven’t won in 50 years. They won strongly Republican seats in Virginia, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, and many other places. They elected union members and farmers. They’re going to have a massive and truly national majority.

And it wasn’t all about affordability. Remember that Fox News poll that hit in late October showing that corruption, not gas prices, was the top issue on voters’ minds. A Harris poll found that “nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem.” A New York Times analysis found that voters, who typically believe that corruption is a problem endemic to both political parties, have come to associate it with Trump and the GOP.

So voters are expecting action on both fronts. If there is one lesson of this election for Democrats, it’s that they have to stop hewing to this asinine view that they can only do one thing. Enough with the caution. Follow your convictions. Do two, three, four, five things at once. Follow the lead of Senator Rafael Warnock, who told CNN’s Erin Burnett this week, “We can walk and chew gum at the same time.… This is the most corrupt administration in American history, and it is literally costing the American people.” We know that some Democrats—Garcia, Jamie Raskin, Elizabeth Warren, Sheldon Whitehouse—are up to the task. But as a group?

We’ll have to see. People often speak of the risk of overreach after such an overwhelming election result. Point taken. But with Democrats, I fear the risks of underreach far more.

items.title: Angry Trump Unravels as GOPers Openly Admit He Wrecked Their 2028 Map
items.content_text: Republicans are “panicking” about what the midterm debacle has done to their presidential map for 2028, Politico reports. Some Republicans fear Texas is now very gettable for the Democratic electoral college map. Others worry that Ohio and Iowa have reverted to true swing states. One Republican suggests the Trump “brand” has become a weapon against the party. Meanwhile, Trump seethed that if he’d been on the ballot, Republicans “WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE.” He fumed that the stock market downturn is the fault of “Dumocrats.” He suggested he will still vanquish Democrats by delivering gains that are “BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE.” He even raged at America for the “sad” outcome, declaring: “You only have yourselves to blame!” We talked to Paul Waldman, who’s been writing well about the midterm fallout. We discussed why Democratic gains in the South and Rust Belt have hidden significance, how to make them truly transformative, and whether a new Democratic Party is being born. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: POTUS’s History Lessons
items.content_text:
It started with a BlackBerry—that now-defunct wireless device and precursor to present-day smartphones. Photographer and author Peter Adams was interested in how consumer products influence politics, and kept returning to the “BarackBerry,” the vintage silver BlackBerry that President Barack Obama had used during his administration, which was modified for security reasons. How, Adams thought, can I locate and photograph that phone?

As his idea grew into a yearslong project, Adams paid visits to, and photographed presidential ephemera from, the Presidential Libraries operated by the U.S. National Archives and Records Administration. The result is the upcoming POTUS: Icons, Artifacts, and History That Shaped the American Presidency (Abrams). The following pages contain just a few of the book’s most memorable images, from the sobering (the safety plug, kept by Truman, for the “Fat Man” atomic bomb) to the propagandistic (a Hoover campaign light bulb) to the touching (pleas for help written on pieces of lumber sent to the Carter White House during the runaway inflation of the late 1970s).

For some, these artifacts will cue a memory; for many others, they’re a window into a time they may have read or heard about but didn’t witness firsthand. Taken together, the objects are a record of the collective American experience—the type of experience that, thanks to our fragmented political and media ecosystems, we’re increasingly missing out on in the twenty-first century.


LYNDON B. JOHNSON
Television Remote Control

President Johnson used this remote to control the three television sets he installed in the Oval Office, one for each network: ABC, CBS, and NBC.


JOHN F. KENNEDY
Map of Soviet Missile Ranges From Cuba

During the first day of crisis deliberations on October 16, 1962, the CIA briefed President Kennedy with maps like this to illustrate the potential reach of Soviet medium- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles installed in Cuba.


WILLIAM J. CLINTON
Painted Toilet Seat (Saddam Hussein)

President Clinton received this gift in the late 1990s, as U.S.-Iraq tensions lingered after the Gulf War amid provocations and multiple weapons-inspection crises. Using bathroom humor to lampoon Iraq’s dictator, it turns an everyday object into pointed political satire.


HARRY S. TRUMAN
Safety Plug for “Fat Man” Atomic Bomb

This plug prevented accidental arming of the plutonium bomb nicknamed Fat Man en route to its target in Japan.


GEORGE H.W. BUSH
Chemical Protective Mask

After Iraq’s battlefield use of nerve agents in the Iran-Iraq War, coalition forces trained and fought in the gulf with chemical defense gear at the ready.


DWIGHT D. EISENHOWER
Campaign Women’s Gloves, “I Like Ike”

President Eisenhower’s 6.6 million-vote margin of victory was thanks in large part to women. Just 32 years afer gaining the right to vote, women made up more than half the electorate in 1952, and nearly 17.6 million of them voted for Eisenhower.


HERBERT HOOVER
Campaign Light Bulb

This novelty bulb, circa 1928, married campaign publicity to the modernity of electric light. Bearing President Hoover’s initials and the GOP elephant, the keepsake advertised Hoover’s technocratic image and Republican Party loyalty.


RICHARD NIXON
Lockpicks

These simple wrenches were part of the lockpick set seized by police after the arrest of five burglars inside the Democratic National Committee’s Watergate headquarters.


GERALD FORD
Gun Holster

Federal officers seized this holster from the residence of Lynette “Squeaky” Fromme after she attempted to assassinate President Ford in Sacramento, California, in September 1975.


RONALD REAGAN
Jelly Bean Jar

Jelly beans became a popular symbol of President Reagan’s lighthearted persona. He began eating them in the 1960s while giving up pipe smoking, and the habit stayed with him into the White House. Jars of the candy appeared on his desk in the Oval Office, in the Cabinet Room, and even aboard Air Force One. His fondness for the treat soon became part of his public image. Admirers sent handcrafted jars like this one, which he received in 1981.


FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT
Lucky Campaign Hat

President Roosevelt wore this fedora for luck during all four of his presidential campaigns.


GEORGE W. BUSH
Butterfly Ballot

Used in Palm Beach County, Florida, during the 2000 presidential election, this Votomatic voting machine featured a “butterfly” ballot layout that placed candidate names on facing pages but offered only a single center column of punch holes. This confusing interface led to frequent “wrong-hole” punches and the now-infamous “hanging,” “dimpled,” and “pregnant” ballot chads—errors that many observers concluded inadvertently diverted thousands of votes to Reform Party candidate Pat Buchanan. The resulting controversy over voter intent prompted Palm Beach County to abandon the layout and led the United States to retire most punch card systems under the Help America Vote Act of 2002.


BARACK OBAMA
Desk Plaque, “Hard Things Are Hard”

During the contentious effort to pass the Affordable Care Act, senior adviser David Axelrod ordered President Obama a moment of perspective, remarking that “hard things are hard.” Axelrod later commissioned this small plaque bearing the phrase and presented it in 2011 to the president, who displayed it on the Resolute Desk for the remainder of his time in office.


Excerpted from the new book POTUS: Icons, Artifacts, and History That Shaped the American Presidency by Peter Adams. Published by Abrams.

items.title: In Memoriam: The Cybertruck
items.content_text:
The Cybertruck, the vehicle of choice for guys who like to say “my pronouns are U, S, and A” and—if they ever did find a woman who wanted to have sex with them—would throw an absolute fit over being asked to wear a condom, is being taken out back and told to think about the rabbits after only three years on the market.

Elon Musk—the Tesla CEO most recently in the headlines for spending half a billion dollars to have his ass handed to him in the midterm elections by a blue wave of young progressives and populists whose platforms weirdly did not include any of his pet issues like “starting a race war”—announced that Cybertruck production would be “winding down” on X, a social media platform he bought in 2022 so as to render it absolutely useless for virtually anything except nonconsensual pornography and shitposting.

According to Musk (the world’s most reliable narrator), this change is simply “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” Totally by coincidence, “Cybertruck sales declined 48 percent from 2024 to 2025” and were down 28 percent from January through September 2026, as the Associated Press reports. All Tesla sales nosedived at the start of 2025—“its worst showing since 2022 and ... far lower than analysts’ predictions”—numbers Wedbush Securities described as “a disaster on every metric.”

Visually, the Cybertruck asked and answered pressing questions. Questions like: What if a hammerhead shark were also a microwave? What if the abstract concept of “toxic masculinity” took on a physical form? Can a car be so powerfully off-putting that it makes your wife divorce you? Can a person communicate, solely through their chosen mode of transit, where they were on January 6, 2021?

We do not yet live in a society where we can recall cars for being hideous. But no matter: Within six months of its debut, the Cybertruck was recalled four times for more material concerns, namely that the construction of these trucks was exceptionally shoddy and likely life-threatening. Trim pieces on the truck bed could detach, becoming a road hazard, as they were not properly adhered to the vehicle; a light bar could also detach and be a risk to other motorists and pedestrians. In April 2024, nearly 4,000 Cybertrucks were recalled after it was found that the accelerator pedal could become stuck—I’ll let you put duh and duh together on the likely consequence of that pesky hiccup. Last March, Tesla had to yank nearly every single Cybertruck off the road because of a stainless steel exterior panel that could fly off and, you guessed it, injure and/or kill people.

But even when construction went according to plan, the Cybertruck was destined to be a deathly menace. Safety experts argued that the stainless steel truck was dangerous by design—they didn’t say anything about how it was also really ugly, but I just think that bears repeating: It’s so unbelievably ugly—but Musk, demonstrating his characteristic empathy and concern for his fellow man, assured would-be Cybertruck drivers, “If you have an argument with another car, you will win.” Famously, car crashes have “winners” and “losers” and everyone’s ideal scenario in a car crash is not only to “win” but to also have committed vehicular manslaughter.

Musk evidently did not consider that Cybertrucks would also endanger their own drivers and passengers, but they did: When only 60,000 Cybertrucks had been sold, there had already been five known fires involving four harrowing fatalities. As The Guardian reported, “Cybertrucks have locked passengers inside and burned so hot they’ve disintegrated drivers’ bones.”

Trapping passengers inside its fire-prone vehicles and burning them alive is something of a Tesla specialty, but the particulars of the Cybertruck’s design were even worse than Musk’s average offering. The windows—ironically, given that during a launch event, an attempt to demonstrate the windows’ impenetrability resulted in them shattering onstage—are tougher to break than a standard car window, which is all well and good until you are trying to, say, escape from a burning car when the doors won’t unlock, as was the case in a horrible crash in Piedmont which killed three college students who “asphyxiated in a fire that had exploded at the truck’s front hood after the collision.” A witness who tried to help them was unable to open the car doors, whose electronic buttons weren’t functioning. (There are no door handles on the outside of a Cybertruck.)

Tesla Cybertrucks are (or, I should say, were) produced in Texas, a state which Musk tried, and failed, to keep in Republican hands. Instead, Democrats won literally every statewide office. James Talarico became the first Democrat to win statewide office in more than 30 years and Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott in the governor’s race—and, per the New York Times: “Every county in Texas shifted left.”

The Cybertruck is survived by Musk, whose unconscionable wealth—net worth: $860 billion, give or take—means he has the means to torment us once more with whatever dumb fucking idea he has next, unless someone in our maybe-soon-to-be-functioning government wants to do something about that. Still, it is important to take our wins where we can get them, and watching Musk fail is one such victory. In trying to embody the spirit of Henry Ford, Musk succeeded only philosophically (by being a Nazi) but not practically (by building a functioning automobile).

items.title: Stephen Miller Will Drag the GOP Further Into the Electoral Abyss
items.content_text:
As a high school student, Stephen Miller once told a booing crowd of his classmates that he was “sick and tired of being told to pick up my trash when we have plenty of janitors who are paid to do it for us.” Now he gets to reckon with a colossal political mess of his own making as the next White House chief of staff.

President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Miller, his deputy chief of staff and domestic-policy advisor, would take the top job in a post-midterms shakeup starting on Monday. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” Trump said in a post on his personal social-media website. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff—She has done a great job!”

Friday’s announcement came after Trump and Miller had effectively handed control of Congress to the Democrats. Two years of disastrous results on corruption, immigration, tariffs, and the Iran War alienated enough of the electorate that Texas went blue after 40 years of GOP control. Now Trump may have just handed Democrats the White House in 2028 as well by promoting his most extreme and destructive advisor to oversee the last two years of his presidency.

The shift was met with applause in the most far-right corners of American conservatism. “Stephen Miller is a wartime chief of staff,” Brent Scher, the editor-in-chief of The Daily Wire, said on Twitter on Friday. “This is going to be awesome.” Benny Johnson, a far-right YouTube personality, wrote on the social-media website that White House aides kept texting him “it’s Miller time” after the news broke. “It’s like the dogs have been let off the chain,” he added.

As Trump’s top domestic-policy advisor, Miller has functioned as a servile but ruthless shadow president for a chief executive who cares more about television footage than policy details. Like all authoritarians, Trump has attracted a mixture of thugs who revel in violence, weaklings who crave service to bullies, and opportunists who hope to advance their own fortunes. Miller has championed the deportation of as many immigrants as possible from the United States, taking an extreme approach even by GOP standards that evokes ethnic-cleansing campaigns and white nationalism.

Miller is also hostile to the American constitutional order and to international law. He argued unsuccessfully for Trump to suspend habeas corpus to round up immigrants last year and told CNN’s Jake Tapper in a January interview that the U.S. should acquire Greenland by force. “We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” he said, in remarks that would not sound out of place for a mid-20th-century German speaker.

His own leadership qualities are hardly stellar. Miller has a reputation throughout D.C. for openly berating junior staffers and senior officials alike for not effectively executing his draconian policies. A 2020 New Yorker profile recounted how he ended one such meeting with Department of Homeland Security officials by emotionally letting down his guard. “I didn’t mean to come across as harsh,” Miller reportedly confessed, describing his obsession with deportations. “It’s just that this is all I care about. I don’t have a family. I don’t have anything else. This is my life.” (He is now married with four children.)

During Trump’s second term, he escalated a series of immigration raids in Los Angeles in 2025 by reportedly telling federal immigration officials to arbitrarily gather people off the streets. “Miller came in there and eviscerated everyone. ‘You guys aren’t doing a good job. You’re horrible leaders.’ He just ripped into everybody. He had nothing positive to say about anybody, shot morale down,” an unnamed DHS official told The Washington Examiner last May, recounting a meeting that he had attended. “Stephen Miller wants everybody arrested. ‘Why aren’t you at Home Depot? Why aren’t you at 7-Eleven?’”

The snatch-and-grab tactics that DHS officials pioneered in Los Angeles and other major cities throughout 2025 came to a deadly conclusion this spring. Miller had championed the administration’s siege of Minneapolis, where thousands of federal agents poured into the city and began grabbing suspected immigrants off of the streets at will. Massive protests and community actions disrupted some of the raids as Minnesotans tried to protect their neighbors. One federal agent shot and killed Renee Good, a writer with three kids, as she tried to drive away from one clash in her neighborhood in January. Another agent gunned down Alex Pretti, a local nurse, who tried to render medical assistance to a woman that the agent had knocked to the ground.

Footage of the shootings and protests prompted an intense public backlash to Trump’s immigration policies. Millions of Americans were horrified at the sight of masked federal agents gunning down their fellow citizens in the street with no consequences. Miller was not among them. He described Good and Pretti as “domestic terrorists” and forcefully advocated for the administration’s tactics in Minneapolis throughout the campaign. After other Republicans begged him to change course, Trump wound down most of the operation shortly after Pretti’s killing and fired Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem a few months later. Miller stayed put.

Miller has often argued in recent years that Democrats are “not a legitimate political party,” but rather a “domestic extremist organization.” Nonetheless, his elevation is good news for Democrats in the short and long term. Trump had initially struck a rare conciliatory note in the wake of the GOP’s crushing losses this week. He accepted the election results after more than a decade of election denialism when things didn’t go his way. His administration’s half-hearted, half-baked efforts to challenge ballots and candidates in Alaska, California, and elsewhere faded away overnight.

“We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them,” Trump told two New York Times reporters in a phone call on Election Night, referring to Democratic leaders. “We’ll probably work something out.” Similar messaging from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer led to growing rumbles in Democratic circles about whether they should be elected House speaker and Senate majority leader, respectively, when the new Congress takes over in January.

A defter and more chastened Trump might have made life difficult for Democrats in Washington by trying to compromise with them, dividing a fractious political party that is normally united in opposition to him. Miller’s promotion has brought that potential honeymoon period to a close. “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries said in a post on Twitter on Friday. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Trump’s announcement is also the first major shake-up of his administration’s top ranks since Democrats recaptured Congress by overwhelming margins on Tuesday. The president said he wouldn’t dismiss Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Thursday despite calls by conservatives for him to step down or be fired. Democrats and Republicans alike blame him for the disastrous course of the Iran War. Outgoing Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, a frequent Trump critic, plans to bring an impeachment vote against Hegseth later this month. Congressional Democrats are reportedly eager to target him with oversight hearings next year as well.

Indeed, nearly all of Trump’s second-term departures have been women. Secretary of Labor Lori Chavez-DeRemer resigned over reports of the toxic, harassment-fueled workplace that she allegedly cultivated. Trump dismissed Attorney General Pam Bondi for failing to prosecute his enemies and botching the Epstein files scandal. Noem was shuffled out of her role after the failed siege and occupation of Minneapolis, as well as a variety of corruption and personal-misconduct scandals. Kimberley Guilfoyle, the president’s son’s ex-girlfriend, lost her job as ambassador to Greece for soliciting payouts in writing from foreign billionaires in September. Katie Zacharia, a woefully inept hire who falsely described her legal credentials, only lasted four days as White House press secretary last month.

Trump’s chiefs of staff also have a tendency to not stick around for long. Wiles was the fifth person to serve in the position so far. The role is a stressful and grueling one under any president. Only three of the twenty-five people to hold the post since 1981 have served for an entire four-year term, and none have done it in the last twenty years. Most do not even make it to a second year. Wiles’ tenure was the second longest one of Trump’s tenure, and was awarded to her in thanks for masterminding Trump’s re-election campaign in 2024.

A White House chief of staff’s power and responsibilities can vary. Generally speaking, they oversee the political staff at the White House. They coordinate policy decisions by the president and various other portions of the executive branch. They liaise with Congress and foreign officials. They go on cable news shows and talk to reporters behind the scenes. Some chiefs of staff, like Jim Baker under Reagan or Rahm Emanuel under Obama, can become nationally known figures in their own right, wielding more influence than even top Cabinet officials.

Like her fellow Trump-era predecessors, Wiles fell on the weaker end of the spectrum. Trump is notoriously capricious and mercurial. He is prone to trusting long-time sycophants like Miller over newer faces and more experienced voices. John Kelly, who served as Trump’s second chief of staff during his first term, later publicly warned Americans ahead of the 2024 election described the then-ex president for whom he had worked as a fascist and predicted that he would govern like a dictator if re-elected that fall.

Indeed, during the first half of his second term, Trump exulted in his lack of constraints—thanks to a MAGA-stocked executive branch and congressional Republicans’ supine posture—and simply did whatever he wanted. By most accounts, Wiles had comparatively little influence to other prominent Trump allies. She found herself overshadowed by Elon Musk, the South African-born billionaire who destroyed federal agencies and laid off civil servants in the first few months of 2025, and by Miller himself, who oversaw the Trump administration’s sprawling mass-deportation agenda.

Now, Miller gets to supervise the wreckage of his own mistakes. He enthusiastically championed Trump’s tariff policy, which drove up prices for Americans and wiped out entire markets for U.S. agriculture and manufacturing. After the Supreme Court struck down most of the tariffs in January, he denounced the justices in the majority as “cowardly.” Even many devout MAGA enthusiasts regarded the Iran War as a betrayal of Trump’s promise to avoid wars in the Middle East and prioritize American interests. Miller has vocally defended Trump’s decisions even as the economic and political fallout doomed his fellow Republicans at the polls.

For Democrats, Miller represents all of the Trump administration’s worst decisions—its authoritarianism, its bigotry, its arrogance, and its foolishness—in one person. There is little doubt that Miller will continue to push the second Trump administration down its self-destructive path, and that he will drag the rest of the GOP down with him. Vice President JD Vance, the putative GOP frontrunner for 2028, gets to spend the next two years publicly defending every extreme decision that Miller makes even as the electorate demands a new course. Other Republicans on the campaign trail will have to decide between embracing Miller’s unpopular policies or distancing themselves from an angry, vengeful power center of far-right American conservatism.

Past presidents have spent the last two years of their administration trying to make things a little easier on their party and their successors. George W. Bush faded out of public view in 2007 and 2008 to avoid tarring the rest of the GOP with his deep unpopularity after the Iraq War and Hurricane Katrina. Bill Clinton, stung by the Lewinsky scandal and his then-historic impeachment, rarely appeared on the campaign trail in 2000 as Vice President Al Gore sought to turn the page. With Miller at the helm, there will be no quiet twilight for the Trump era. The two men will continue to inflict as much harm as they can on the country—and, by extension, on any remaining hope for the GOP to stay in the White House or reclaim power in two years’s time.

items.title: Trump Runs Away as Reporter Reminds Him He’s a Big, Giant Loser
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump scurried away from reporters Friday who asked about his new loser status.

Trump had an awkward interaction with reporters outside the White House after they asked him to explain his decision to replace chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller.

“I wanted to make a change,” Trump said. The president had previously dismissed reporting that he was planning to oust his “ice maiden”—but that was before Republicans suffered staggering losses in the midterm elections this week.

“We gotta make moves, sometimes in life you gotta make moves,” Trump said.

“We’ve beaten Iran. We are doing very well with Iran, we are talking to Iran, we have been. We haven’t lost a soldier in seven months, or six months,” Trump said.

In July, just four months ago, Trump attended a funeral for four U.S. service members who were killed in Iranian attacks in the Middle East, amid reports accusing the Trump administration of hiding casualty numbers. As of October, 23 soldiers had died as a result of Trump’s disastrous military campaign.

Trump quickly departed from the press gaggle, as one reporter shouted after him, “How does it feel to lose?” The president continued to flee and did not respond.

items.title: Trump Plans to Accuse Nonprofits of Having Terrorist Ties
items.content_text:
When in doubt, call them a terrorist. The White House is tapping into its standby strategy in its latest attempt to cripple nonprofits.

Donald Trump is weighing an executive order that would brand some nonprofits as having terrorist ties, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday. In doing so, the executive order would nix the organizations’ nonprofit status and fundamentally unravel their operations.

Sources familiar with the matter told the Journal that the executive order has been in the works for months and is not yet finished. It remains to be seen if Trump signs the effort or scraps it altogether.

It was not immediately clear which groups could be targeted, though the dangerous label could offer a much more immediate route for the administration to penalize its perceived political opponents than by pursuing potential legal violations through the IRS.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hinted that such an effort was underway while speaking before the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism in mid-July.

“We are examining where tax-exempt status has been exploited, which charitable entities have become financial conduits for foreign-influence activity, and how those entrusted with stewardship of these organizations have instead enabled violence,” Bessent said at the time. “Where the evidence leads, we will not hesitate to follow.”

Nine organizations have already been identified as having terrorist ties, though those designations came from federal agencies such as the Treasury Department, as opposed to from the White House, according to the Journal.

But there have been numerous other occasions in which Trump and his allies have baselessly resorted to the “T-word” to advance their agenda. Earlier this year, officials across the Trump administration branded Minneapolis residents Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti as terrorists in order to brush their deaths at the hands of federal agents under the rug. And even in the most recent election cycle, Republicans resorted to slandering Representative Ilhan Omar and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed as terrorists in futile attempts to discredit their authority and undermine their influence.

items.title: Democratic “Moderation” Isn’t What Produced the Wave
items.content_text:
You can watch this episode of Right Now With Perry Bacon above or by following this show on YouTube or Substack. You can read a transcript here.

The midterms were not a story of Democratic moderation, political scientists Adam Bonica and Jake Grumbach argue. Instead, they say that Democrats won everywhere due to strong turnout among left-leaning voters, weaker turnout among conservatives, and some voters flipping to Democrats because of anger at President Trump. Increased Black turnout in the South and Latino voters in the Southwest swinging back against Republicans were particularly huge factors, according to the two scholars. The two emphasized that Democrats across the country won by employing an anticorruption message. Looking forward, Bonica, who teaches at Stanford University, says Democrats can take actions to address corruption and billionaire power within the House of Representatives and other institutions they will control, without needing Trump’s signature. Grumbach, who teaches at the University of California, Berkeley, says the results are the latest indication that all kinds of candidates can win elections. Therefore, in upcoming primaries, Democratic voters should focus on policies and candidates they like, rather than polls and perceptions of electability.

items.title: Transcript: Democratic “Moderation” Isn’t What Produced the Wave
items.content_text:
This is a lightly edited transcript of the November 5 edition of Right Now With Perry Bacon. You can watch the video here or by following this show on YouTube or Substack.

Perry Bacon: Good afternoon. This is Right Now on The New Republic. I’m the host, Perry Bacon, joined by two regular guests at this point, two of my favorite political scientists. Adam Bonica is at Stanford, Jake Grumbach is University of California, Berkeley, and this is our second podcast where we’re going to break down the election results and talk through them some. So Adam, Jake, thanks for joining me.

Jake Grumbach: Thanks for having me.

Bacon: So let me start with, when I talked to you all about doing this, I wasn’t thinking about discussing Mississippi. And really didn’t think about South Carolina either, to be candid about it. So I definitely had in my head 52 Senate seats, 230. That was what all the data experts were saying. And I think NBC had over 250 estimated.

So let’s talk about that first in terms of your general impressions. I’ll start with Adam and then go to Jake. Your general impressions of what we saw on Tuesday.

Adam Bonica: I had expected 250 seats. And that was way above. And even that, the size of the wave—no one predicted it would be this large. No one predicted Mississippi would be in play.

And one thing I thought was probably pretty clear is that it was unlikely that we would see a situation where we would just have a few races that were really close. It was probably going to be in the Senate either a big win or a pretty devastating defeat. It was much more bimodal than we’ve seen in the past.

But the other thing is this majority is going to rival the size of the majority Democrats came into office with after 2008. The year in which they were able to get a lot done. And it is surprising. I think we’re all still processing it.

Grumbach: Yeah, I agree with Adam. I’m sorry, I’m a little choppy right now. I’m having some computer difficulty, so I’m a little choppy right now, but I hope you can hear me.

I was surprised at this wave election. The one thing I’ve learned from Adam over the years is that in the modern polarized era, parties rise and fall together in wave elections. And this was a blue wave election, that across the country you saw massive blue shifts, and the wave was big enough that it carried even parts of the Deep South. It looks increasingly like it’s going to include Mississippi. Of course, Texas was a massive sweep by the Democrats.

But for me, I think one of the most underemphasized pieces of this has been Black organizing in the South. I served as an expert witness for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, pre-Callais, in a Voting Rights Act case in Mississippi. And as a Northerner, I’m a Californian through and through, my impression of Mississippi being there was that it was unlikely to shift blue anytime soon, despite the efforts of Black people in Mississippi and the occasional caucusing coalition with white liberals as well.

So I think this was a real national wave election, and that’s the main takeaway, is that the Democratic Party fielded pretty good candidates across the board, across the country, that were compelling in their areas, and that the Republican Party under Donald Trump is incredibly unpopular.

Bacon: So I want to do a little bit about geography now. You talked about the South a little bit, but is that the big geography story? Or is there anything else about geography we should think about?

Bonica: I think the geography story has been one long in the making. So when all is said and done, I think the story of this election, one of the stories in terms of demographic shifts, is going to be, A, a turnout story, where we’re going to see that Democrats finally matched or exceeded Republican turnout rates. And two, that the youth vote was incredibly important.

And this has been a trend, right? When young people turn out and show up for Democrats, they tend to win in wave elections. That’s been the pattern since 2008, really.

And if you looked at Mississippi, if you looked at Texas, you saw these generational curves that were overwhelming. And a lot of the backsliding, I think we saw, the Democratic backsliding that Jake has written about, the gerrymandering, the pushing democratic institutions away from electoral democracy to preserve these majorities, had a lot to do with the fact that there was this generational pressure building in Texas, even in Mississippi. Mississippi has a big curve, too. The younger people in Mississippi were pretty Democratic.

And we saw it happen first in Georgia, but Texas and Mississippi, they’re not as unpredictable as one would think. I think it happened sooner than I would have expected. But the geography story, again, I think is really more a geography story about how young and old people in a lot of these states have very different sort of partisanship and preferences.

Bacon: Jake, I asked while you were away about if there’s a geography story of the election. I think the one story we’re talking about is the South. But is there any other geography story? And also, if you want to talk about the South more. Because I think that’s the takeaway, was Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas. Talk about that story. What do you think is driving that?

Grumbach: First, apologies for my technical difficulties. This seems to happen every other Perry Bacon show session I go on. Won’t happen again, I’m investing in better hardware.

So I do think Adam’s right about a geography story, but overall I’ve really learned from Adam that national waves carry the day, and this was true of much higher turnout among Black voters and young voters than previous midterm elections outside of potentially 2018.

Adam talks a lot about differential turnout. So swing voters do matter here. A number of people did switch from voting Trump 2024 to in 2026 voting the Democratic slate in their areas. But really across the country it’s that Republicans were more likely to stay home, people who lean Trump or wouldn’t ever vote for a Democrat but are now a little bit disappointed or embarrassed by the MAGA sort of performance.

And increased turnout and passion from Black voters as a response to the Voting Rights Act ending, Latino voters as a result of the economy, the cost of living and ICE, and young voters who see a Democratic Party nationally that provides a potential path forward rather than “Just vote for us, we’re not Trump,” type of thing.

So I think it’s really across the board, but regions do matter, and bigger swings in the redder places, that is places that were deeper red or swung farther towards Trump in 2024. Southwest Texas is a classic. Latinos in West Texas split maybe 50 percent Trump 2024 or so. They absolutely repudiated that coalition in this election, which resulted in a massive swing.

But again, I would say the story is national, and in a wave this big, the biggest wave since Watergate in terms of the popular vote for a single party in a midterm election against a president like this, it really carried the entire country.

Bacon: So I’m old enough to remember stories about there being a political realignment in America after 2024, in which voters of color were going to vote Republican in the future. So I think it’s worth doing a little mockery, but let me be serious for a second here to say, I think one account of that, the account I had of that, was anti-inflation, anti-incumbency.

Biden lost a lot of voters, including voters of color and including young voters, and some of those people are going to come back in 2026. That’s obvious and that was going to happen. So I thought the realignment stories were overdone a little bit.

But that said, the numbers looked a little bit deeper than just a real shift backwards toward the Democratic side. So Adam, was there never a realignment? Did Trump realign again by being so crazy? So talk about the minority story of 2024 and 2026.

Bonica: Yes. So Jake and I, I think we talked about this with you probably a year and a half ago, looking at how turnout was the primary dynamic that mattered in the 2024 election. Places where turnout was depressed tended to be in more urban, more multiracial areas.

And places that saw increases in turnout—Trump, one thing to his credit, is he really does have a turnout advantage. These sort of poll misses seem to consistently follow this trend, that he is able to mobilize a certain part of the electorate that may be less inclined to vote.

So if you take, the turnout dynamics are important, but then there’s another type of voter, which is an anti-system, often anti-incumbency voter, who may be activated because they’re upset about something, but also just they don’t like the status quo, and they don’t like the party in power often, and their vote is against the system.

And we see this consistently as well. The types of voters that are swing voters, and they exist, there are plenty of them out there, they’re not the type of voters who are being persuaded by, “Here I have policy X versus policy Y.” They tend to be people who say, I want my life to be better. I think the system is broken. I think the system is corrupt. And they’re more of a disruptive force, not a sort of orderly, you can be won over by being more appealing than the other side. You win them over by right now not being the party in power.

Bacon: When you say turnout, let me probe a little bit. It is obviously the case that more people voted in 2024 than 2026. That’ll be almost the case, I’m sure, in every state. So when you say turnout, drill down. What I think you mean is, in Chicago, more people voted for Joe Biden in 2020 than voted for Kamala in 2024. So therefore, this idea that individual Chicagoans did not become Republicans who are Black.

And so roughly, the Republican Black people in Chicago turned out, some of the Democrats didn’t, and it creates a swing that is really turnout-based. But I think in like South Texas, there was actual swing, right?

Bonica: Yeah. And this is partly why South Texas stands out so much, why it is the outlier region. I think there are a lot more voters of the type I just described, and they probably had that stacked on top of a turnout differential that looked different.

Think you have 100 Democratic and 100 Republican voters in a district. On average, Democrats historically have been turning out like 60 of them in midterms versus 70 for Republicans. That gap between the probability of a registered Democrat turning out versus a Republican was about as large as it has been in a decade in 2024.

And in 2018, the last time we have full data for, it was about equal. Democrats were equally likely to get to the polls as their Republican counterparts. When you close that gap, Democrats win in big wave elections. And when that gap widens, Democrats perform really poorly in Republican wave elections.

Grumbach: All right, yeah, to jump in here. So Perry, you started talking about the supposed realignments of 2024. You said you think they are a bit exaggerated. They were a lot exaggerated.

So the big things were like, Latinos are now a conservative group that will consistently vote Republican, or lean at least purple to Republican. The second was young men, especially the red-pilled young men, Joe Rogan listener type of kid.

Bacon: Joe Rogan listeners just—

Grumbach: Exactly. That’s just now MAGA. Then you see this cultural dominance in punditry and media. You saw New York Magazine has sent the cruel kids table, and it’s like this election that Trump wins by a couple percentage points becomes this mandate that culturally MAGA is dominant, led by Latinos and young men shifting, right? And that really disrupted this idea of the Democratic Party as this more multiracial coalition that we know historically since really the New Deal and the civil rights era.

But what happened very quickly in 2025 is those constituencies swung back dramatically. As Adam mentioned, there’s differential turnout, so the more conservative Latinos and young people.

This was a classic thing, was that Latinos swung to Trump 2024 somewhat, right? They still were majority Kamala Harris, but the biggest Republican presidential victory for Latinos since George W. Bush 2004, who was much more engaged in Latino outreach than Trump was. And this was like, OK, we’re in post-racial politics. Latinos are rejecting racial politics.

But it actually turned out in surveys that it was the more racially conservative Latinos who were shifting most towards Trump 2024, the types of people that answer survey questions that, for example, Black-white inequality is due to a lack of Black effort rather than discrimination. If you agreed with that statement, you were much more likely to swing towards Trump as a Latino in 2024, or a young man.

What happened after that, though, was a rapid shift backwards. And they’ve co-written some excellent pieces. There’s one in Boston Review laying out how to fight authoritarianism that I thought would give a really good look at why what Schumer and Jeffries are doing is not effective, if you’re trying to win this broader fight. And they have a more recent piece about the consulting class that was published here at TNR. So I encourage you to check out both of them, and great to see you guys. Bye-bye.

Grumbach: Thanks so much, Perry.

items.title: Abdul El-Sayed Launches “Habibi PAC” Days After Winning Election
items.content_text:
Days after defeating Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate election—overcoming $38 million in American Israel Public Affairs Committee funds, a tidal wave of bigotry and Islamophobia, and an eleventh-hour betrayal by Democratic Representative Haley Stevens—Dr. Abdul El-Sayed has launched the “Habibi PAC.”

A Federal Election Commission filing shows that the first Muslim to ever be elected to the U.S. Senate made the PAC official on Thursday. The leadership PAC is not connected to his campaign and will allow him to raise money for other candidates, perhaps a sign of greater political ambitions.

Habibi, meaning “my beloved” in Arabic, is a term of endearment that El-Sayed has used often during his campaign, even using it to refer to Vice President JD Vance in his victory speech early Wednesday morning.

“JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed said.

Abdul El-Sayed to JD Vance:

JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January. pic.twitter.com/4XwZejXsm8

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 4, 2026

items.title: ICE’s Own Report Found It’s Not Giving Detainees Sufficient Care
items.content_text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators determined that failing medical care preceded the deaths of 23 immigrants in detention.

The San Francisco Chronicle obtained internal reports on the deaths of 29 immigrant detainees who died between January 2025 and January 2026. In the 29 cases the Chronicle reviewed, 23 immigrants died after receiving medical care the agency itself found was deficient.

ICE investigators determined that detention staff “deviated from safe limits of practice,” or “did not provide medical care within safe limits of practice” for the 23 detainees.

In at least eight of the cases, medical staff failed to perform CPR correctly, or at all. In only three of the cases, investigators determined that the deficient medical care did not directly contribute to the person’s death.

The agency continues to insist that there has been no spike in detainee deaths, though 2025 saw the most immigrant detainee deaths since 2003. So far in 2026, 31 immigrants have died in ICE detention.

During President Donald Trump’s second term, ICE has subjected tens of thousands of people—including U.S. citizens, lawful immigrants, and immigrants with no criminal convictions—to overcrowded rooms, unsanitary conditions, and insufficient food and water.

In many cases, immigrants report having been denied adequate medical care. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff released a report in October 2025 documenting at least “85 credible reports of medical neglect” at U.S. detention centers. In January, ICE announced that it had stopped paying for immigrant detainees to receive health care—and wasn’t planning on paying again for months.

For the Trump administration, the cruelty is part of the point. The Department of Homeland Security even rejected plans to construct immigration detention facilities that were more humane.

items.title: Trump Promotes Stephen Miller as He Doubles Down on Extreme Agenda
items.content_text:
Stephen Miller will be taking over as White House chief of staff beginning Monday.

Trump made the announcement on Truth Social Friday afternoon, saying that “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Miller, previously the White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, is receiving the promotion after serving in both Trump administrations. He is well-known for his hardline, xenophobic, and racist views on immigration, which led to violent and deadly mass deportation policies in Trump’s second term.

Trump’s decision to elevate Miller suggests that he is unrepentant about much of the negative attention brought by ICE’s violence even after Republicans were dealt historic losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Earlier this week, Miller was the target of leaks from Republicans and Trump administration officials over how his deportation plans were going too far, with even one anecdote about First Lady Melania Trump complaining to the president about people she knew being deported. Wiles reportedly tried for months to steer Trump away from Miller’s approach, according to The New York Times.

Ultimately, though, Wiles is the one on her way out. She tendered her resignation Thursday night, as Trump has partly blamed her for the GOP’s devastating election losses, Wired journalist Hugo Lowell reported. Rumors that she would be made into a scapegoat for the elections had been floating around for weeks.

In a statement posted on X, Wiles said, “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First. More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”

Promoting Miller now is a clear message to Democrats after their massive election victory.

The death of nurse Alex Pretti at the hands of ICE agents in January caused a sea change in Americans’ thoughts on immigration, and gave Democrats the edge this November. ICE heavy-handed tactics continued, though. ICE agents have shot at least 25 people in Trump’s second term, according to the Times. On top of that, dozens of immigration detainees have died in ICE custody due to inhumane conditions encouraged by Miller.

But Trump clearly doesn’t care about any of that, and wants to double down on the most brutal part of his second term by elevating his most vile staffer, giving Miller the run of the White House. Any thoughts of Trump moderating or working with Democrats in the final two years of his presidency have been dashed by this move, and Democrats should receive the message loud and clear.

In response to Miller’s appointment, Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who will be taking over the House Oversight Committee next year, said “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

This story has been updated.

items.title: U.S. Hits Bonkers Measles High as RFK Jr.’s CDC Hides Death Totals
items.content_text:
The U.S. is on the cusp of losing its measles elimination status.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed 5,182 measles infections nationwide Friday, the highest case load of the disease that the country has experienced since 1991. Forty-five states have been affected.

But public-facing federal datasets have not kept up with state reporting. The agency has acknowledged just four measles deaths so far this year, while Pennsylvania on its own has reported six. Health agencies in New York and Wisconsin each reported at least one additional death.

Measles hasn’t been a national concern since 2000, when the long-term use of a vaccine proved so effective at minimizing risk and exposure to the disease that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared measles eradicated from the United States. That status is up for reassessment this month. If it’s determined that a singular viral strain has circulated the country for 12 months, the U.S. will no longer qualify for the label.

The virus’s dormancy has been challenged by anti-vaxers, who have opted against medicating their children in fear that vaccinations could cause autism (a thoroughly debunked conspiracy). One such conspiracist, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has refused to combat the ensuing measles outbreak with vetted science—instead, he has issued guidance that the illness can be treated by simple vitamins.

In April, Kennedy fell short of offering a full-throated endorsement of the MMR vaccine that has historically been used to treat measles, telling CBS News that his agency was focused on finding treatments for unvaccinated individuals while falsely claiming that the jab had not been “safety tested” and was not effective for long-term prevention. As of 2025, there are no known effective treatments or cures for measles other than vaccine prevention.

The return of historically eradicated diseases is thanks to a growing movement of anti-vax parents who refuse to provide their children with the same public health advantages that they received in their youth, mostly in fear of giving their children autism. The researcher who sparked that myth with a fraudulent paper lost his medical license and eventually rescinded his opinion. Since then, dozens of studies have proven there’s no correlation between autism and vaccines, including one study that surveyed more than 660,000 children over the course of 11 years.

But America’s is not the first measles response that Kennedy has bungled. Under Kennedy’s stewardship, the anti-vax nonprofit Children’s Health Defense had its own questionable history with the disease. Preceding a deadly measles outbreak on Samoa in 2019, the organization spread rampant misinformation about the efficacy of vaccines throughout the nation, sending the island’s vaccination rate plummeting from the 60–70 percent range to just 31 percent, according to Mother Jones. That year, the country reported 5,707 cases of measles as well as 83 measles-related deaths, the majority of which were children under the age of five.

items.title: Democrats Put Tech Giants That Courted Trump at the Top of Target List
items.content_text:
Democrats are eyeing investigations into some of America’s largest corporations that tried to curry favor with President Trump. 

The Washington Post reports that now that Democrats won back control of Congress, they are planning to probe powerful entities in Wall Street and Silicon Valley, and the first targets could be Apple, Meta, and Elon Musk and all of his companies. 

The House is already preparing to investigate how President Trump used Musk’s artificial intelligence chatbot Grok in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, according to the Post. House Democrats are also looking at Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and at Meta for demanding that local governments sign nondisclosure agreements regarding data centers. 

Corporate lawyers in Washington, D.C., are scrambling to meet with corporate executives to offer advice on the impending high-profile public investigations. Many firms are preparing pitches to attract Musk as a client, as he is not only the world’s richest man, but also holds billions in government contracts, has a close relationship with Trump, and led the disastrous Department of Government Efficiency initiative.  

One lawyer at a major D.C. firm told executives in a private online meeting Thursday that “this is a new era.”

“If your company is caught up in this oversight, it’s likely to be much more highly publicized,” the lawyer said, according to the Post. 

Dozens of corporations and CEOs donated to Trump’s transition fund, his inauguration fund, and his White House ballroom project. Where that once may have protected them from regulations and investigations from the Trump administration, with this new Congress, the opposite is true. Trump also made millions investing in many companies and publicly praised companies that did him favors. 

“Lawyer up,” wrote Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, the next chair of the House Oversight Committee, in a brief statement on election night.

items.title: Stunning Map Shows Just How Much the Country Swung Left in Elections
items.content_text:
Want to see just how far left the United States shifted in Tuesday’s midterm elections? Look no further.

A map produced by Ground News using data from civicAPI showed just how far each U.S. county’s margin moved from the 2024 presidential election to the 2026 House vote. A whopping 94 percent of U.S. counties shifted left in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Jurisdictions in all 50 states reported an average 13-point shift toward Democratic House candidates. No state showed an overall shift toward the Republicans in the House, although there were a handful of districts that moved right.

The states that showed the largest shifts toward Democratic House candidates were New Jersey, Utah, West Virginia, and Wyoming. The states that saw the smallest leftward shifts were South Dakota, Vermont, and Oregon.

The map indicated that even in states where Democratic candidates did not win, such as West Virginia, Indiana, and Kentucky, there were still heavy leftward shifts among voters.

Voters under 30 swung sharply toward the Democratic Party, according to the AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters across all 50 states. Republicans appeared to lose most—if not all—of President Donald Trump’s gains with Hispanic and Black voters in 2024. Moderate and lower income voters also turned up to support Democratic candidates.

items.title: Trump Official Doug Burgum Has Been Pushing Data Centers for a Reason
items.content_text:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has been pushing to build artificial intelligence data centers on public lands since he first joined President Trump’s Cabinet. A Friday report from ProPublica shows that Burgum might feel so strongly about the centers not because of worries about China or the future—but because he has somewhere between $18.1 million and $64.4 million invested in artificial intelligence companies.

Burgum’s 2026 financial disclosure document shows that the vast majority of his wealth is held with Arthur Ventures, the investment firm he co-founded. While Burgum’s Senate confirmation ethics agreement forced him to resign from Arthur Ventures, he still maintained his financial interests at the firm. According to an analysis by public lands advocacy group Save Our Parks that was shared with ProPublica, Arthur Ventures invests between $18.1 million and $64.4 million in AI companies—meaning that Burgum is pushing an unpopular policy that will personally enrich him. Burgum has blamed the mass rejection of data centers on a “foreign psyop.”

The Trump administration, of course, denies ProPublica’s reporting.

“Secretary Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations,” a U.S. Department of the Interior spokesperson said. “Any suggestion that his office decisions are driven by personal investments are false and completely unsupported.”

Yet Burgum isn’t the only Trump administration member who stands to personally profit from his investments in AI and data centers. According to a ProPublica review, over 380 administration members or their spouses have investments in or other financial ties to Nvidia, 320 have ties to Alphabet, and over 240 are invested in Meta Platforms—all while the administration allows states to construct data centers and inject their technology into every level of everyday life unfettered.

“Like every other goon in this administration, Data Center Doug is in it for himself,” California Representative Jared Huffman wrote online. “He wants to cover our public lands with AI data centers that will make him and Trump’s tech buddies richer.”

items.title: Amy Acton Says She Won’t Speak to Vivek Ramaswamy After Beating Him
items.content_text:
Dr. Amy Acton is washing her hands of Vivek Ramaswamy and his dirty campaign tactics.

Ohio’s first female governor-elect told CBS Mornings Friday that she has “no intention” of speaking to the losing Republican after he produced a disturbing political advert featuring her estranged mother.

“It was sad, I would like to say I didn’t expect this but there was no low my opponent wouldn’t sink to,” Acton said, noting that Ramaswamy’s other attack ads were filled with “lies” and “vitriol.”

“I heard that he did leave you a congratulatory phone call,” said host Gayle King. “Have the two of you spoken since election night or at all?”

“Gayle, I think we can’t normalize behavior like this. It was so beyond the pale. So I have no intention of speaking to him. I do believe that leaders’ words matter, and we need to hold folks accountable,” Acton said.

As the days ticked down to the midterm election, Ramaswamy hatched a crackpot plan to damage Acton’s credibility by weaponizing the sexual assault she suffered during her childhood against her. Ramaswamy used Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, as part of a smear campaign to paint the Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee as a liar.

He moved forward with the ad spot against the advice of his team, and while ignoring publicly available information demonstrating that Arthur abandoned her children to skip town with her husband—Cledith “Bud” Arthur—who was indicted for allegedly raping Acton when she was a young girl.

The biological daughter of that man lent credibility to Acton’s account of the abuse days after the smear campaign was leaked. Speaking through tears during an interview with the Daily Mail, the Youngstown, Ohio–based woman said that Arthur had also raped her late sister, Christine, years before he married Acton’s mother.

Acton has been very public about her broken family and childhood struggles. Over the years, she has discussed the horrific sexual abuse she endured from her stepfather (which she told The Youngstown Vindicator occurred between the ages of nine and 12), and also shared her experiences with homelessness in her youth. In a March 2020 profile by The Toledo Blade, Acton said that she spent one of her childhood winters living in a tent outside Youngstown.

Ramaswamy—a biotech billionaire that attended one of Ohio’s largest private high schools—saw those stories as potential political fodder, and attempted to utilize them for his own personal gain. But in doing so, he ultimately hurt himself.

The 41-year-old MAGA acolyte has since become a bit of a political pariah that is unwelcome on either the left or the right, as Democrats and Republicans alike condemned the low blow.

items.title: Trump Aides Are Eying the Exits After Disastrous Elections
items.content_text:
Donald Trump’s midterm bust has even his White House aides eyeing the exit.

“There is no holding back on the desire to leave now,” one former White House official told MS NOW Friday. “Some are making calls to try and jump ship.”

What happened on Tuesday has been described by some Republicans as an “extinction-level” event, as Democrats scooped up areas of the country that have been historically seen as deep-red, according to the news outlet. A White House official told MS NOW that the election results had amounted to “the worst-case scenario.”

But as Trump approaches the lame duck portion of his second term, some members of his staff are looking for an off-ramp out of MAGA world.

“In this current trajectory, there’s no shot this is salvageable,” a former White House official in touch with current staffers told MS NOW, speaking on the matter of the MAGA agenda. “What is the president’s focus these last two years? It’s probably renovations.”

Trump has obsessed over his legacy throughout his second term, a fixation easily illustrated by the long list of vanity projects he’s cooked up instead of fulfilling the difficult job of steering the nation. So far, Trump has razed the White House East Wing, started construction on a $600 million ballroom (the price of which keeps growing), proposed a 250-foot “Triumphal Arch,” gutted the Lincoln bathroom, transformed the Palm Room from a lush green foyer into a sterile lobby, and mowed down Jackie Kennedy Onassis’s famous Rose Garden.

The administration also spent more than $16 million on an unsuccessful and rushed renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, took a sledgehammer to the Harry S. Truman Bowling Alley, indiscriminately axed trees in the Washington area, and destroyed the Kennedy Center in a futile attempt to attach Trump’s name to the living memorial.

“There is no holding back on the desire to leave now,” the former official continued. “Some are making calls to try and jump ship.” Others are reportedly seeking out legal counsel as a “precaution,” the official told MS NOW.

Another former official summed up the current atmosphere succinctly: “pain.”

“Everybody’s going to start infighting,” they told MS NOW.

items.title: Two Top Justice Department Officials Jump Ship on the Same Day
items.content_text:
On the heels of assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s departure Thursday, two more leading officials from the Department of Justice are resigning.

Politico reports that John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general in charge of national security, and Jason Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, are both leaving the DOJ. Eisenberg oversaw cases relating to espionage, leak investigations, and terrorism, and was also involved in the prosecution of former Trump national security adviser (turned Trump critic) John Bolton earlier this year for illegally retaining classified materials.

Quiñones oversaw an investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan over his statements to Congress about Russian interference in the 2016 election. Quiñones was also overseeing the prosecution of former Cuban President Raúl Castro. In a statement, Attorney General Todd Blanche said that “We are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime. Jason has served the Department multiple times over his distinguished career, and we thank him for his service to this country,” Blanche said.

Blanche also announced Eisenberg’s resignation, noting that this was his “second tour of duty serving President Trump as a national security official and advisor.”

Democrats’ resounding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections seems to have scared officials in the DOJ, who may now be targets of investigations in a Democratic-controlled Congress next year. Subpoenas and other oversight tools are already being prepared against the DOJ.

Democrats will also be able to look into the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, President Trump’s business dealings, corruption surrounding presidential pardons, and deals with foreign governments—and those are just the tip of the iceberg. Dhillon, Eisenberg, and Quiñones are likely the first of many to jump ship, and they should probably consider lawyering up.

This story has been updated.

items.title: America’s Ugliest Car Is Coming to an End
items.content_text:
The era of Elon Musk’s Cybertruck is finally coming to an end: After years of persistently weak sales, the technocrat’s polarizing mini tanks are officially headed out of production.

Musk announced Friday that Tesla’s Texas plant would cease production in the middle of next year in order to build CyberCab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Since launching Cybertruck in 2023, Tesla has consistently struggled to meet the vehicle’s sales target of 200,000 per year. In the third quarter of 2026, the company only sold 8,300 “other models,” which includes the Cybertruck. Ahead of the vehicle’s initial release, Musk fretted on an earnings call: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck.”

Musk’s metal monstrosities became the unfortunate symbol of Donald Trump’s second term, after Musk bought the president’s way back into the White House in 2024. Musk spent twice as much to buy this week’s midterm elections for Republicans, but he’d have been just as well off if he’d lit the cash on fire.

The announcement comes as Tesla’s shares declined 11 percent Thursday, following a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections that flipped both chambers of Congress blue. Evidently, investors are concerned that Musk could face new congressional probes and harsher regulations. The aggregate market cap losses for Tesla and SpaceX came to more than $420 billion since Tuesday’s close, CNBC reported.

Musk has used his proximity to Trump to boost his many businesses, including Tesla cars, which Trump showed off at the White House like a hacky used car salesman. In some cases, the administration even pressured foreign governments into approving Musk’s products.

Democrats have signaled they plan to investigate Musk’s shady leadership of the defunct Department of Government Efficiency, his companies’ lucrative contracts with the federal government, and his alleged role in cutting Ukraine’s Starlink access, perhaps on behalf of his close friend Russian President Vladimir Putin.

items.title: Trump Obsesses Over Triumphal Arch After Judge Blocks Construction
items.content_text:
President Trump is still fixated on his triumphal arch even after a federal court halted its construction on Thursday.

In a 33-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan wrote that no construction can take place on the arch for 14 days while other legal proceedings play out, which she said were likely to succeed because, unsurprisingly, the Trump administration didn’t follow the legal processes before beginning the project.

The ruling came hours after the National Capital Planning Commission, packed with Trump allies, voted to approve the project in an 8-4 vote, ignoring eight hours of comments opposing the measure from concerned residents, veterans, and lawmakers. But there are multiple lawsuits hoping to stop the project for good: one from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, as well as a joint lawsuit from the District of Columbia and Virginia governments.

Meanwhile, Trump seems unphased. The official White House X account posted an AI rendering of the arch on Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., Friday morning along with a link to triumphalarch.com, a website full of Trump’s praises and reasons for the project.

The project’s opponents have complained about how the massive building will overshadow Arlington National Cemetery and obstruct the view of the Lincoln Memorial. But Trump doesn’t care about that, or what the courts say about his project. He also seems to be disregarding the message Americans sent in Tuesday’s elections, as he pushes ahead with an unnecessary vanity project and his party is left in shambles. Meanwhile, Democrats are gearing up on how to stop him.

“I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it, because, in case you hadn’t heard, we’ll soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously,” Democratic Representative Jared Huffman warned at the planning commission meeting Thursday.

items.title: Laura Loomer Goes on “Hiatus” After Bombshell Revelation on Paid Posts
items.content_text:
Right-wing influencer Laura Loomer announced she is taking a “brief hiatus” from her Loomer Unleashed podcast just hours after a Trump administration adviser exposed her for being paid to post some of her manic, hateful content.

It all started on Thursday, when Alex Bruesewitz, who is behind much of Trump’s digital media strategy, took aim at conservative social media influencers following the GOP’s massive midterm election loss.

“Believe it or not attacking Democrats over their relationships with a streamer (Hasan Piker) wasn’t an effective hit,” Bruesewitz posted, not mentioning Loomer by name. “GOP candidates probably shouldn’t take messaging advice from fringe right-wing ‘influencers’ moving forward.”

Loomer took the bait.

“But they should take their advice and meetings with @TuckerCarlson instead?… It’s completely reasonable for people to be appalled with Democrat candidates campaigning with a guy who said America deserved 9/11. Hasan Piker regularly makes comments in support of jihadi groups,” she wrote. “What wasn’t helpful was your friend Tucker Carlson essentially endorsing Abdul El-Sayed over Mike Rogers and using his show to tell people to not support Rogers just a few weeks out from an election. But we all know you will never condemn your buddy Tucker.”

“Laura, you are basically the Republican version of Hasan Piker. Democrats over the years have attacked Republicans for affiliating with you. Those weren’t effective hits either,” Bruesewitz replied. “Voters simply don’t care enough about ‘influencers’ or streamers. lol”

Loomer took offense to that, claiming that she was not an influencer and criticizing Bruesewitz for his association with Omeed Malik, a conservative venture capitalist and major Republican donor.

“I’m a journalist and an opposition researcher Alex. What are you? What is it that you do for Omeed Malik exactly? He’s a Muslim right? Half Iranian and half Pakistani if I’m not mistaken,” Loomer fired back. “Is that why you have such an issue with the things I say about Islam?”

“Okay lol. But is it common for journalists to get paid for their opinions and tweets?”

“You say ‘Okay lol.’ Not sure why you are laughing. I recall last year your company X strategies reached out to me asking me for help. Do you deny that? What is so funny? I guess I don’t get the joke,” Loomer said, admitting that she was indeed paid to tweet. “You loved sharing my journalistic reports during the 2023/2024 DeSantis-Trump primary too. What changed?”

“No I don’t deny that. I’ve paid you for tweets before. I haven’t for at least a year though,” Bruesewitz wrote back. “I also know you still get paid by others for tweets so I do think it’s fair to refer to you as an ‘influencer.’ What percentage of your tweets are paid for?”

Loomer had no direct response to Bruesweitz’s question, instead accusing him of having ties to the Qatari government.

This a massive allegation, further confirming that much of what we see on social media is privately paid for and manufactured by people with a particular political bias.

Hours later, Loomer announced a “one to two month show hiatus.”

“I’m getting married, and I want to give this exciting part of my life the time that it deserves, as I’ve spent a lot of time fighting for our country, and for President Trump—sometimes at the expense of my own personal life,” she said.

The hiatus, of course, also comes after Loomer posted 119 times on X in less than 28 hours following the election results, according to an analysis by Newsweek.

While some online chalked up Loomer’s break to the Republican midterm upset, others noted that it also occurred right after the revelation about her undisclosed paid content. We still don’t know how much she might’ve been paid, or who else is paying her.

items.title: The Question Now Isn’t About Democrats. It’s What Will Republicans Do?
items.content_text:
Everyone is focused, and understandably so, on the question of how aggressive the Democrats will be in investigating President Donald Trump, his administration, and his enablers. But the actual main question that now confronts America in the wake of Tuesday’s Republican bloodbath is a different, and very simple, one. Will elected Republicans recognize the new reality and begin to return to the planet that the rest of us occupy, or will they continue in their supine servility to the man who brought them to this cataclysmic point—and who will do untold damage to this country and world in these next two years if they don’t help rein him in?

Before we start to answer that question, let’s check its premises, because history overflows with people asking the wrong questions. Its premises are two. First, that we have entered a new reality. Have we? And second, is it in fact Trump who is responsible for the Republicans’ cataclysm?

On the first premise, the answer is an emphatic yes. The election results are so overpowering that they transcend mere politics. This is a cultural change. There are moments in politics when you can just feel a dam bursting, when you can just hear a democratic people collectively screaming, We’ve had enough!

I’m old enough to remember, and honest enough to confess, that 1980 was definitely such a moment. It wasn’t even Ronald Reagan’s landslide victory, though that was evidence enough. It was the flipping in the Senate of 12—yes, 12—seats, with numerous old liberal lions like Birch Bayh and Frank Church losing to no-name Republican contenders who were of a new and decidedly more right-wing breed than Washington was accustomed to at the time. I still remember watching the returns that night and thinking, Hmmm. Something is happening out there that I didn’t understand at all.

On the second question, the answer is—well, it’s an even more emphatic yes. Vice President JD Vance can blame the midterm rout on the Iran war. Please, God, let that settle in as the conventional wisdom on the right, because it will doom them to further failure. This bloodletting happened because of Trump: the war, sure, but also the tariffs, the economy, the corruption, ICE detentions and killings, the hiring of his harlequinade of incompetents, the ballroom, the Reflecting Pool—all of it.

Pollsters are paid to settle on one explanation, so they do what confused pols seeking clarity pay them to do. But the world and people’s brains don’t work that way, especially when a leader insists on making us think about him as incessantly as Trump does. Trump, in his unquenchable sleaze, malfeasance, corruption, and economic incompetence, just became too overwhelming for the average voter. Anyone who thinks this sea change was about anything else is lying or stupid.

Very well. We’ve addressed the premises. Now let us return to the question itself. Now that Trump is about as lame as a lame duck can get, will congressional Republicans finally rise up against him in defense of reality?

It’s the most important question of the moment because, tragically, under the rules of the modern media, Republicans will still have more power to stop him than Democrats will. Yes, Democrats will hold the committee gavels, and Democrats will have more power over subpoenas and witness lists and all the rest when it comes to congressional oversight hearings. That’s real power, and they should—and by most accounts will—use it.

But we must presume that Trump will ignore, and will order all his people to ignore, the Democrats’ subpoenas.
