Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is almost certain to be the next House speaker, likewise said that the party will be united “right out of the gate” to address the cost of living crisis—a topic that Democrats credit for their massive Election Day wins. In a “Dear Colleague” letter on Thursday, he proposed reversing cuts to the Affordable Care Act subsidies that have forced millions of Americans to pay more for health care, undoing cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, reversing tariffs, and stopping the war in Iran—all in the first 100 days of the next Congress.

Some advocates are pushing Democrats to start even sooner. “Government funding runs out on December 11, and I think they should use that must-pass vehicle to demand an end to the war in Iran, bringing down gas prices. And they should ensure that the Medicaid cuts don’t go into effect in January, which would raise health care costs for families,” said Lindsay Owens, executive director of Groundwork Collaborative.

Republicans, of course, might not go along with that while they still hold power in the lame-duck session. There’s also the issue of President Donald Trump’s veto power, which could thwart Democrats’ affordability legislation during the next Congress. Trump has given conflicting messages, telling some journalists that he plans to work with Congress and others that he will become “Mr. Veto.”

Some Democrats want to tailor their agenda to that reality. “How about we spend the majority of our time on stuff that we all agree on,” Representative Adam Gray of California told Semafor. Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii is similarly cautious: “I do not think it is time to propose things that the president of the United States is guaranteed to veto,” said Schatz, who is in line for a Senate leadership role. “I think that’s a bit of wasted energy.” Progressives like Representatives Greg Casar of Texas and Ro Khanna of California, on the other hand, adamantly disagreed with that sentiment. “Make him veto Medicare for All. Make him veto a $25 living wage. Make him veto free childcare. Make him veto Block the Bombs to Israel,” Khanna wrote on X.

Economists like Josh Bivens, chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, also want to see Democrats go beyond just addressing the high cost of groceries and gas, which was a major part of the campaign. “In terms of the policy levers that will actually work to make affordability better,” he said, “we have at least as many, probably more, that work on the income and wage side than the price side.”

Raising the minimum wage and passing labor legislation that empowers workers would increase incomes. It would be a way to give Americans more purchasing power without trying to lower the cost of goods directly, which can be more difficult. Jared Bernstein, chair of the United States Council of Economic Advisers under former President Joe Biden, makes a similar argument, and is concerned that Democrats could overpromise and underdeliver on lowering prices. “Nobody should be saying that they can lower the price of everything within the walls of Target and Walmart,” he said. “Trump, of course, made precisely such claims, and to say they redounded against him is a massive understatement.”

One thing that most Democrats and experts can agree on: ending the Iran war as quickly as possible. Even if ending the war doesn’t immediately bring down the price of gas, it would begin the process. The war is deeply unpopular; in a remarkable social media post on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance admitted that it’s part of why Republicans lost Congress.

Even if Trump’s vetoes make affordability legislation tricky, Democrats “have another tool, and that’s oversight,” Owens said. “Americans are aware that one of the reasons that prices are so high is corporations are charging them more than they need to, taking advantage of the war in Iran, taking advantage of the tariffs to raise prices,”she said. Addressing and exposing corporate corruption, she argued, is also good affordability politics. Ultimately, Democrats will need to think about the full array of tools at their disposal—lowering prices, raising incomes, pressuring Trump to sign their bills, and holding hearings. Perhaps the most important thing they can do is show voters that they are doing whatever they can to make life more affordable.

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

Could Dems’ state-level victories turn out to have a greater long-term impact than retaking Congress? While the tally is not yet final, Dems so far appear to have ended Republican “trifectas” in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas; built Democratic trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and possibly Arizona; flipped the North Carolina House, quite possibly the Texas House, and both chambers in New Hampshire; and won the governor’s races in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas. “Democrats will have the power to rewrite policies on redistricting, abortion, climate, health care, education and taxes,” The Washington Post summarizes in its rundown of state results. That includes taking “meaningful steps on lowering utility costs, expanding access to child care and health care, reproductive rights, safeguarding elections and other issues.” And then there’s the big question that Axios raised this week: Could Dems’ state victories pave the way for getting rid of the Electoral College?

Let’s zoom in on one item in the Post’s list: What do these sweeping Democratic victories mean for climate policy? The party conspicuously sidelined the issue on the campaign trail. But as Steven Rodas and Liza Gross at Inside Climate News pointed out this week, voters consistently backed environmental protection on state and local ballot measures on Tuesday. Perhaps the most striking example: More than 80 percent of Michigan voters chose to ban campaign contributions from utility companies. (The first lawsuit challenging this ballot initiative has already been filed.)

The new Democratic trifecta states in particular now have a lot of options on the climate front. And there are signs of movement at the national level, as well: Chellie Pingree, fresh off a commanding victory delivering her a 10th term in Maine’s 1st congressional district, is ready to rumble, telling Grist’s Jake Bittle this week that she has, in Bittle’s words, “prepared a long list of investigations and subpoenas for Trump administration officials, including EPA chief Lee Zeldin.” Pingree, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations subcommittee that oversees the Environmental Protection Agency and Interior Department, also wants to insert stipulations in funding bills “that would deny agencies core operational funds or restrict travel money for leading officials unless they doled out solar and energy funding as Congress previously instructed them to.” For an administration famously attached to its travel money, that probably counts as shots fired.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

On Monday at 2 p.m., the Brookings Institution will host an online event about “the consequences of the 2026 midterm elections,” featuring David C. Barker, Karen Tumulty, Jonathan Rauch, and Sarah A. Binder.

Also on Monday, at 1 p.m., New America will host a virtual discussion with Better Life Lab’s Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson about their new research on men and caregiving, as well as insights regarding the barriers that keep some men from being more involved in caregiving, even when they want to be. Mohan Sivalogonath of Dads for All, stay-at-home dad Shannon Carpenter, and elder caregiver Carlos Olivas will join for a panel discussion.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Good Week: 

I mean, there’s an obvious answer here: Literally almost every Democrat. But if we think outside the box, then we might have to hand this award to Mike Johnson, who announced after the midterms that he would not be running for minority leader, one of the worst jobs in Washington, perhaps second only to being the majority leader in a GOP-led House. Johnson led a caucus of MAGA-werewolves who routinely brined themselves in right-wing meme slop about as well as anyone could. He will now get to spend more time with his son and their favorite hobby: monitoring each other’s pornography intake.

Bad Week: 

Again, obvious answer: nearly every Republican in Christendom! But some Democrats fared poorly, as well. Haley Stevens’s decision to go against the party and endorse Mike Rogers was a shot so poorly taken that even Lin-Manuel Miranda would have been like, “Hales, I’d have holstered that one.” And we must spare a thought for John Fetterman, a senator who exists only to thwart his own caucus, which will now swell to numbers so large as to make him entirely irrelevant. Go ahead and switch parties, pal! (Caveat: A new annoying Democratic senator with swing vote power could emerge at any time.)

—Jason Linkins


Political Trivia Question of the Day  

The first Latino governor in the United States was Romualdo Pacheco of California. In what decade did he ascend to that office? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: American Taxpayers on the Hook for Ivanka Trump’s Lavish Birthday Trip
items.content_text:
Ivanka Trump, the president’s daughter, got to take a nice birthday trip to Marrakesh, Morocco, with taxpayers helping to foot the bill.

The Daily Mail reports that Trump was spotted walking through the streets of the city on October 29, one day before her forty-fifth birthday. The newspaper obtained federal records showing two Secret Service contracts adding up to $93,000 for agents to secure and stay in two five-star hotels ahead of Trump’s arrival.

These included a $59,543 contract for rooms at the five-star Sofitel Marrakech, and a $33,457 contract for a Secret Service team at La Mamounia, where the Kardashian family and Winston Churchill have stayed. Those bills don’t include agents’ transportation, meals, flights, or salaries.

Officially, Ivanka Trump is not a White House employee, but she is entitled to Secret Service protection as a child of the president. The trip was reportedly not long, as the Daily Mail’s source said that she returned to the U.S. in time for Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Moroccan news outlet Le360 said that Trump was seen walking through Marrakech’s old neighborhoods and souks, and ate traditional Moroccan food. It’s her third visit to the country, according to the news outlet, as she visited on a diplomatic trip in November 2019 when she was an employee of the first Trump administration, and later in summer 2022 on a private trip with her husband, Jared Kushner.

Ivanka Trump’s net worth is estimated at $100 million. Even though she is entitled to Secret Service protection, at a time when many Americans are struggling (thanks to her father’s policies), she should be willing to reimburse the government for all of the high-end expenses she racked up in Morocco, as five-star hotels don’t come cheap. But perhaps we should be grateful that she didn’t stay at a Trump-owned property and force the Secret Service to fork over money to the family business, like her father often does.

items.title: White House Is “Monitoring” Conservative Groups Amid Break With Trump
items.content_text:
After a disastrous midterm showing that placed the future of the MAGA movement in abject peril, the White House decided it was a good time to let conservative groups know that they were being watched.

A Thursday memo from the White House Office of Public Liaison sent to about 3,000 conservative organizations listed a series of Trump accomplishments, vowing that a Democratic Congress wouldn’t reverse them, according to The Wall Street Journal. But the memo ended with one sentence highlighted in yellow: “As always, we are monitoring statements, press releases, and media engagements from your organizations.”

“‘We’re watching you’ is not the message the White House should be sending,” Caroline Sunshine, a White House aide during Trump’s first term, wrote online. “We’re LISTENING to you is what anyone in the WH who has the President’s best interest should be saying.”

Earlier emails from the White House office didn’t include language about “monitoring” groups, according to a review by the Journal. The shift comes as a flurry of conservative voices, from commentator Matt Walsh, to Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, to Vice President JD Vance himself, have lambasted President Trump’s policies and decision-making—placing sole blame on him for Republicans’ midterm election loss. And while the office told The Wall Street Journal that it wasn’t a threat, this is an ominous message to send to a coalition that is actively fracturing.

items.title: Transcript: Trump Shivs Hegseth in Weird Aside as GOP Knives Come Out
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 6 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Donald Trump’s war on Iran played a major role in the GOP’s massive electoral drubbing this week, and as a result, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in serious trouble. Donald Trump just defended him, but then in a strange aside seemed to suggest he’s vulnerable. Meanwhile, Republicans and Trump allies really have their knives out for Hegseth, and the campaign to remove him appears serious. He even faces an impeachment vote next week.

But we want to get into what the Democratic Congress can really do about Hegseth’s disastrous reign. So we’re talking to Congressman Adam Smith of Washington State, the incoming chair of the House Armed Services Committee. Congressman, thanks so much for coming on.

Adam Smith: Well, thanks for having me, Greg. It’s always a pleasure.

Sargent: So, on Hegseth’s tenuous position, ABC News’ Jonathan Karl spoke to the president and reported Thursday that Trump said, “I have every intention to keep him.”

But Trump said people unhappy with Hegseth aren’t contacting him, saying, “I get these calls about him. I don’t understand why.”

And Trump even admitted it would be easier to confirm a new defense secretary before Dems control the Senate next year.

Congressman, this is how Trump turns on people, with talk like this. You’ve been around the Pentagon a long time. How do you read it?

Smith: I think it’s 50-50 that Trump does get rid of Hegseth for the reasons you stated. And also because the Iran war has been a complete disaster. Trump needs a fall guy. And we all know Trump’s not going to take personal responsibility for it.

So Hegseth would be convenient, and deservedly so. Hegseth was a cheerleader for this and a lot of the disastrous decisions that have been made going into it, Hegseth has been right in the middle of. So I think that’s a distinct possibility.

The other thing to weigh here is that on Wednesday the motion by Congressman Massie is ripe for a vote. And by every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.

Sargent: That’s going to be quite a scene. And MS NOW reports that Trump has been asking allies what they think about Hegseth, and some of them are pushing for a replacement. One official says, “There’s a lot of people who want his scalp, and they smell blood in the water.”

This looks real to me, Congressman. What are you hearing from inside the Pentagon? Is there consternation?

Smith: Yeah, well, we don’t hear a lot from inside the Pentagon. I can tell you, from inside the military more broadly, yes. There are people who have been concerned with the way Pete Hegseth has been running the department. And it comes down to politicization of it, first of all.

And second of all, it’s become so much about personality. Look, there is a professionalism within the military. And that’s not that there aren’t people who serve in the military who don’t have strong political views one way or the other. There certainly are. But they’ve always put those aside in favor of the job, the mission, and working together.

Pete Hegseth has not done that. I mean, he’s had those two, you know, ridiculous forums where he brought every flag officer together to give a pep rally of sorts, in which he seems to be obsessed with physical appearance more than with actual results.

We’ve had the firings that, from what we’ve heard, in many instances people have no idea why they happened. Hegseth is the first secretary of defense ever to directly involve himself in mid-level promotion decisions, you know, to go in and cross off names.

So all of that, I think, has had a very negative effect on morale within the Pentagon. And look, none of this is to say that there aren’t some people, I’m sure, in the military who love Hegseth and love what he does. But dissatisfaction within the Pentagon about his leadership is high, from what we have heard, or what we’ve been told.

Sargent: I’m sure it is. I’m sure there would be a lot of people who’d like to see him go.

The Iran war has cost $47 billion so far. Trump is still talking about a major attack. Have you been briefed on what the attack is? Senator Murphy says it’s “insane.” Is he right?

Smith: Yeah, I mean, look, they haven’t briefed us consistently on this from the very start. They have been doing attacks in the last few days, last few weeks.

What isn’t widely understood is, for months now, we have been engaged in a major military operation to secure safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Now, yeah, we’re up close to, like, 80 percent of traffic of what was there before the war. But it’s costing us an enormous amount of money to protect those ships coming through, and to bomb potential missile launchers and missiles that Iran’s trying to build. So it’s become very, very expensive.

Sargent: Can you talk a little bit more about that? Because it seems like there’s a vulnerable pressure point here for Democrats going forward. How much are we talking about? How much is being spent just to escort these ships out of the strait?

Smith: I don’t know exactly, because they won’t report it. And that’s the lack of transparency we’re talking about, and the lack of information that Hegseth just isn’t providing to us. But you see the dollars and the figures adding up, and it is definitely having a huge impact on how the Pentagon pays for everything else.

And also, where does it end? Iran does not appear to be interested in giving up anytime soon. So how long can we keep this up? And this isn’t even talking about all the bases that we’ve had damaged and destroyed in the Middle East, which are not calculated in that $47 billion, by the way.

Sargent: Do you think that there’s a massive cost here that’s being buried?

Smith: Yeah, no question. I mean, the equipment that has been destroyed and the bases that have been destroyed have not been calculated into that cost. That’s just what we’ve spent.

Sargent: Democrats are going to have to get that information, right?

Smith: Yeah, that’s going to be one of our big pushes, is to get some transparency and get some information provided.

Sargent: So how are Democrats going to stop this war? Is there a coming point at which they’ll need money and can be defunded there?

Smith: There’s no easy way to do it, because Trump keeps robbing every account he can rob to keep funding it and keep moving it forward. What we will do is we will vote resoundingly to end the war. We will vote to cut off all funds that go to the war. But remember, he will still be president. He will still have veto power.

I think the war can be stopped if we can persuade a number of Republicans. We could conceivably get a two-thirds majority to do this. And maybe Trump finally wakes up and starts caring about what people think instead of just doing things on a whim. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that one.

But the other part of this is, we have to end the war, but to end the war, we have to admit something that we’re not going to want to admit. We lost. Iran will be in a stronger position when this war is over than they were when it started. And we will be in a weaker position. And that’s just baked into the cake at this point.

There’s no fixing that. And historically, we stayed in Vietnam too long, we stayed in Afghanistan too long. And part of the reason was, well, we don’t want to admit that we lost.

Sargent: Trump certainly doesn’t. So just for clarification, you think that Democrats in both houses next year will pass a measure which cuts off funding, in the sense that it forbids funding for the Iran war?

Smith: Absolutely. I think it’ll be one of the first things we do, and strongest things that we should do.

Sargent: And then I think there is a case to be made for then trying to get some Republican support to override the inevitable veto. But this will be a bill, if I understand you correctly, which forbids the use of any funding for this war.

Smith: Yeah. That would be the plan. And obviously, look, the legal language and the loopholes and the ways that Trump can sort of jump out of it, those will all continue to be challenges. But yeah, the war has been a disaster. It needs to end.

But a lot of the damage has been done. It’s not like we end the war and everything goes back to normal. Another thing that we need to really push is diplomacy. I mean, right now, Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Iran are talking. Because this, it’s horrible for us. It’s horrible for much of the country. But it’s really horrible for the people in the Middle East who are having to endure this constant and spreading war.

Sargent: I think there’s a scenario you can envision that looks a little something like this. Maybe you pass this thing out of both houses. You even get a couple of Republicans, I don’t know, in the House, maybe, although all that’s left is the really hardcore people at this point on the Republican side.

But you pass it and it cuts off funding, Trump vetoes. Maybe you go to Republicans and say, why don’t you guys go to the president and tell him that you’re going to vote for this thing unless he exits it quietly, or give him a way out, give him an off-ramp, right? Is there a scenario like that? I mean, you’re a veteran of this stuff.

Smith: That should be happening right now. There should be some kind of a negotiation happening. This is not going to be easy for us to get out of.

Sargent: So I want to ask you about a few things that need to be investigated. The Pentagon hasn’t released the investigation into the U.S. bombing of the girls’ school in Iran, which killed dozens and dozens of kids. What’s the Armed Services Committee going to do next year to get that?

Smith: Yeah, we will continue to put pressure on them to release it. We’ve been doing that in a bipartisan way, and thus far they have rejected doing that, which is a huge challenge.

Sargent: Subpoenas?

Smith: Yeah, potentially. But yeah, we can subpoena them, we can hold them in contempt. The report should be released. I mean, it’s been nine months now.

Sargent: There’s a strong case to be made to Republicans in Congress who have called for it: Well, OK, you want the report, you say you want the report. Well, join us in supporting a subpoena of it, right?

Smith: Yeah, we will try that, to be sure. Look, one of the things that’s going to be really hard for all of us to deal with is, we’ve taken back Congress, certainly, but Trump is still president.

The executive still has a lot of power. Trump ignores Congress. Trump ignores the courts. This is going to be a very, very difficult fight, and we’re going to have to consistently push to try to get some of the changes that we want.

Sargent: Well, that’s where defunding comes in, I think. My sense is that Democrats are going to have to get a little more comfortable than they are usually with using the defunding lever. Because this is a lawless president. If there’s ever a case for using that defunding pressure to force lawful behavior, this is it.

Smith: Sure, but we do have to be careful. You’re talking about defunding the Pentagon?

Sargent: No, more targeted. More targeted things. Like, I think the start would be for both houses to cut off all funding for the war, and then maybe start to slightly escalate.

Smith: Yeah, no, I think that’s probably a good place to start.

Sargent: Well, the U.S. continues to kill people in boat strikes in the Caribbean. The last one was on October 4. Well over 200 people have been killed at this point. Little to no evidence is being released that these are even drug smugglers.

You’ve criticized this, other Dems have criticized this. Now you’re going to have power. Is there going to be a deep and serious investigation here that gets to the bottom of how this bombing campaign came into existence? Who pushed it, who authorized it, who resisted, what’s the evidence, so forth?

Smith: Yes, we are going to attempt to do that. Absolutely.

Sargent: Can you talk a little bit about what that looks like? What do you try to establish in this?

Smith: Well, I mean, I think we want to establish the justification for it. And we’re going to want to bring in people who have made decisions around it, just like you described, and get some explanation. But crucially, Where is it going? What’s it trying to accomplish? What’s going to happen here going forward into the future?

Sargent: Right. And is defunding these strikes an option? I mean, let’s say they come back with—

Smith: Yes.

Sargent: OK, what would have to happen for that step to be taken?

Smith: The same thing, I think, as on the war in Iran. We have to pass, no fund is authorized for boat strikes in Latin America. And then we’d have to face the president’s veto.

And I mean, look, before we get into all of that, I think there is going to be a legitimate effort on our part to say, hey, can we do this the easy way? Can you change these policies that are manifestly unpopular? Can you stop the war, stop the boat strikes, and move in a different direction? While at the same time being prepared to use those stronger levers that you described.

Sargent: I do want to ask you a little bit more about these stronger levers. The administration’s going to defy your subpoenas. So you’re going to subpoena people to appear and discuss the boat strikes. You’re going to subpoena people to release or discuss the report on the bombing of the girls’ school.

Trump’s going to tell people not to testify. This is my speculation, but it seems reasonable to expect that there’s going to be intense obstruction. They’re going to throw subpoenas in the garbage.

There will have to be, in a general sense, a little more of a comfort level, I think, about using the defunding lever. I’m wondering if you could just kind of talk about whether you think Democrats have to get to that point a little bit.

Smith: Well, we do. I mean, as I said, we need defense money, and pass legislation that says, no funding shall go to these particular purposes. And we’ll have to have that fight. Look, it’s going to be an ugly fight between Congress and the executive branch for the next two years. There’s no question about that.

Sargent: How far do you think you’re going to get? Do you think you can get that report on the girls’ school released? Do you think you’re going to be able to stop the boat strikes? Will you stop the war?

Smith: Look, I really don’t know. I mean, and if I said I knew—anyone who says they know, it’s just—we are headed into uncharted territory here. The Trump presidency is absolutely unprecedented. He is completely unresponsive in a way that no other president has been, even after the shellacking that they took in the election.

I mean, you saw Clinton when he lost in the midterms in ‘94, he pivoted. You saw Bush even pivot after losing in 2006, certainly saw Obama pivot after we lost in 2010. What’s Trump going to do? It’s unprecedented. So we’ve got to try to figure out what he’s going to do. And, you know, so it’s going to be a major challenge.

Sargent: I do wonder whether the war can actually be defunded successfully here, or whether it’s going to actually have to come to that.

Smith: Yeah. No, look, the one thing I hope people understand is, the damage that Trump has done is not easy to unravel. Because even if you sort of dig down a little bit on what ending the war means, you know, we pull out, we pull back, what happens then? That’s why I think the diplomatic element, the peace negotiations, are such a crucial part of this. But it’s going to be a challenge.

Sargent: Do you think that if it actually comes to a defunding fight, like if everything you’ve tried has failed and you vote to cut off funding for the war, do you think the leadership will be supportive of that, the Democratic leadership in Congress?

Smith: Yes.

Sargent: Do you have, like, special assurance of that, or is it just speculation?

Smith: I think ending the war is one of our central pledges in this election.

Sargent: Yeah, it has to be done. It would be a catastrophe if Democrats punted on that, don’t you think?

Smith: Absolutely. Yeah. But again, the problems are complicated. You know, Trump has dragged us into a conflict that’s going to be problematic.

Sargent: Yes, it looks that way. You came out for impeachment of Donald Trump the other day. You want to just make your case?

Smith: Yeah, look, I mean, he’s out of control. He’s not a normal president. What he’s doing is not normal. He’s incredibly dangerous. He has defied over 250 different court rulings. He ignores Congress. He is corrupt beyond imagination, enriching himself, raffling off pardons, the whole Bitcoin stuff, his family.

So all of that is terrible. But the bottom line is, as long as he’s president, we can’t really trust that he’s not going to do even more incredibly damaging things. So that’s the big concern.

Now look, I’m mindful of the fact that a lot of our new members in the House are going to come from districts that don’t want impeachment. So we’re going to have to have this conversation about what’s best for our caucus. And I will follow our leadership. I’m not going to try to undermine them.

I think we need to try to have a cohesive—unity is an overstated way of putting it—but we’re going to have right around 260 members in the House. Getting some sort of cohesive agreement on where to go is a key part of this.

Sargent: I wouldn’t want to be in your shoes, Congressman. Let me just ask you, speaking about all these outer-tier members, these members from districts that Trump carried by eight, nine, 10 points, do you think at the end of the day they will be willing to support whatever it takes to end the war?

Smith: I don’t know. I don’t think they know. I mean, look, how to put this exactly? This election was primarily about, well, a couple different things. One, how terrible Trump is. His policies, certainly, but also just his general demeanor and attitude.

We had candidates all across the country who were just decent people, who said, enough of this nastiness. You know, let’s get back to working with our neighbors, trying to figure out how to make things work better.

And then there were Trump’s policies, the tariffs, the immigration crackdown, the war in Iran and huge feeling amongst the American people that life in America fundamentally isn’t fair. And so you could go out there on the stump and you could say, I’m a farmer, I’m a veteran, I’m a teacher, I understand our community, I’m with you, I’m going to help you, I’m going to help protect you. But what does that mean in terms of policy?

We’re $39 trillion in debt. Yeah, we need to get rid of the Medicaid cuts. We need to get rid of the Affordable Care Act cuts, a lot of other cuts. How’s it going to be paid for? Are people in favor of the tax increases that are going to be necessary to get us there? How are we going to accomplish those things, given the hole that has been dug? Certainly by Trump, but even before Trump, we just put ourselves in a weaker position that made the whole thing more difficult.

Sargent: Are there clawback options that you think should be exercised to try to fund the restoration of Medicaid and stuff?

Smith: Yeah. I think we should repeal the entire One Big Beautiful Bill, which means we should put taxes out there. But we have to, I believe, as Democrats, make the case that tax increases are not always bad. All right? If we can’t make that case, then we’re going to have a difficult time delivering on our promises in terms of how to help people.

Now, and part of that is all the billionaires and multimillionaires, all the money that has gone there instead of being available for the programs we need. But those things are going to be difficult. And like I said, I think the people who run for office, they’re great people and everything, but the actual legislative solutions are going to be a lot harder.

Sargent: It certainly is going to be extremely challenging and extremely tense stuff. Congressman Adam Smith, thank you so much for coming on with us. Great stuff. We really appreciate it.

Smith: Thanks, Greg. Thanks for the chance.

items.title: The CIA Men of Wild Horse Nine Are Sorry
items.content_text:
In writer-director Martin McDonagh’s debut film, In Bruges, two hit men hide out in the eponymous Belgian city, waiting for a call from their boss. The older man, Ken (Brendan Gleeson), loves playing the tourist. “Bruges is the most well-preserved medieval town in all of Belgium, apparently,” he recites from his guidebook. His companion, Ray (Colin Farrell), disdains the provincial pleasures of what he calls “fucking Bruges.” “I used to hate history, didn’t you?” he says. “It’s all just a load of stuff that already happened.” But Ray is so racked with guilt over a botched hit, no wonder he’d rather pretend the past didn’t happen. The only problem is that he sees it everywhere he looks.

Wild Horse Nine, McDonagh’s fifth and most recent feature film, is structured a lot like In Bruges. Both center on two men wandering through an exotic locale, largely unimpressed, frustrated by one another and consumed by regret. The order to kill or be killed forces one of them to choose between personal loyalty and professional duty. For the men of In Bruges, this duty is to the ethical code of the hit man. In Wild Horse Nine, contract killers have been replaced by CIA agents, glorified mercenaries who are bound to protect not democracy so much as American interests.

Wild Horse Nine isn’t just built like a McDonagh movie: It sounds and thinks like one too. Having started his career as a playwright with The Beauty Queen of Lehane and The Lieutenant of Inishmore, McDonagh still writes the kind of dialogue—witty, too witty at times—meant to be played to the back row. The billboards in Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri constitute a near-haiku of minimalist free verse: Raped while dying / And still no arrests? / How come, Chief Willoughby? In response to his wife’s postcoital dirty talk in that movie, Chief Willoughby (Woody Harrelson) jokes that he thinks he’s heard that line in a Shakespeare play. “You dummy. It’s Oscar Wilde,” his wife (Abbie Cornish) flirts back.

It is that tension between sweeping cinematic vistas and peculiar, theatrical language that produces McDonagh’s signature effect: pleasing, jarring, a bit off kilter. To watch these actors proclaim their odd thoughts, impeccably expressed while roaming the dusty Midwest or the streets of a medieval city or the vividly saturated Irish coast is to recall how all the world’s a stage, and all the men and women merely players (hint: not Oscar Wilde this time).

In Wild Horse Nine, set in the early 1970s in the wake of a string of dubious ops, CIA agents Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell) are invaders, colonizers, sowers of chaos and violence across the globe and even, we discover, at home. Are these men deserving of their outsize influence, deputized, as they are, by the U.S. government? Not at all. They only approach something like worthiness once they realize they should never have had such power in the first place.

The result is a film more nuanced in its understanding of American exceptionalism than Three Billboards, more political than In Bruges, and just as beautifully lonely as The Banshees of Inisherin. Then again, as Lee half-heartedly tells his friend, “It’s lonely everywhere if you’re gonna die, right?” And if there’s one way we know for sure we are in a McDonagh story, be it a play or a film, it is that death is waiting in the wings.


The main action of Wild Horse Nine takes place on Easter Island. The Moai statues feel tailor-made for an auteur obsessed with dismemberment as a metaphor, providing an immediate dose of violence while promising more bloodshed to come. Anywhere from 500 to 800 years old, the Moai direct stony glares at tourists, but Lee and Chris are not cowed; they irreverently refer to them as the “big heads.”

This odd couple has landed here because Chris said he wanted to see the Moai before he died. He doesn’t remember this wish, though Chris, suffering from cancer-induced dementia, is liable to forget he is dying at all. What Chris knows, and what he has been letting slip in these final days, might get him killed before his illness finishes him. At the very least, his insensitivity will tank his chances at an Easter Island hookup.

Though Chris is the one on a journey, stricken with guilt at the end of his life—for all the deaths he has caused or for which he has been in the “general area”—Lee is the one with a choice to make. Will he murder his friend because he has asked him to do so before his illness becomes untenable, or will he murder his friend because his boss, MJ (Steve Buscemi), has asked him to? “I wish I could die knowing I could trust you,” Chris remarks. It is an impossible dilemma, patently absurd, which is to say, textbook McDonagh: Silly moments are tainted with dread, and doom and death are shot through with silliness.

The film’s central  dilemma is patently absurd, which is to say, textbook McDonagh: Silly moments are tainted with dread, and doom and death are shot through with silliness.

Chris poses a special threat to the agency because he has chosen to write a memoir, which would, presumably, cover his involvement with the agency-directed hit of America’s thirty-fifth president, John F. Kennedy. “How’re you gonna write that memoir if you can’t remember anything?” Lee inquires. Chris, unbothered, decides to begin his book with a discussion of a dinosaur afterlife, asking Chris, “Didn’t they have, like, vegetarian dinosaurs?” (Wild Horse Nine, keeping company with the 2011 The Tree of Life and this summer’s The End of Oak Street, proves that, when one’s own past proves too burdensome, dinosaurs have the power to bridge the gap between right now and back then, our personal traumas and our shared cultural memories.)

The first third of the film feels light, almost surface-level, as characters banter about beautiful women, unfaithful wives, and which countries have the best cheese (the gayest countries, Chris insists). It makes sense that, in a film about state secrets, talking in code, and cognitive decline, we might feel, as viewers, that something is being redacted. But, as MJ turns the screws on Lee and Chris decides he actually wants to die in, in his words, “Venice, Italy,” the film becomes darker and more claustrophobic. At a bar, Chris tells the two Chilean students they have befriended (Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas) not to go back to their country ahead of what will be the 1973 Chilean coup. He details the horrors to be inflicted on scores of young leftists, their friends and family, and warns them, “Never let them get you in the car,” advising her, instead, to “die in the street.” The allusion to this unspeakable violation earns him a slap across the face, though this warning later proves prescient and invaluable.

While McDonagh’s previous film, The Banshees of Inisherin, is as sweeping as a fairytale, Wild Horse Nine feels more like a play, with its limited settings: a nondescript hotel room, a CIA office, the tacky ordinariness of a 1970s home. It is the disembodied Moai, looking on in judgment, that provide the film’s most compelling visual hook, together with a Kodak Ektachrome–inspired aesthetic. Lee and Chris, dressed in muddy oranges, yellows, and browns, clash with the panoramic swaths of clear blues and greens of Easter Island. The film’s evocatively dated look can be attributed, first, to cinematographer (and regular McDonagh collaborator) Ben Davis, who filmed in a combination of digital and 16mm/super-8 film, and to the makeup team, who curated the delightfully clownish makeup looks for Lee’s wife, Marge (Parker Posey).

And, like a play, Wild Horse Nine relies on its performers above all, with long takes and even longer monologues, pronounced against relatively blank staging. Rockwell, a McDonagh regular, turns in a heartfelt performance, cranky but sincere, and plays well with Parker Posey (another White Lotus alum), who executes her small, messy performance with precision. Buscemi is appropriately menacing, though he is even better playing his character’s weaselly vices for comic purposes. But the film belongs to John Malkovich, with his odd speech cadences, his unnerving glare, and his ability to shift, seamlessly, from levity to murderous violence.

One of the most memorable moments in the soundtrack, played as the two men drive across Easter Island, is Judy Collins’s sweet, melancholy 1967 rendition of “Both Sides Now.” “I’ve looked at life from both sides now,” she sings, but it is “life’s illusions” she recalls. For most of Chris’s career, he has forced himself to believe, as Lee puts it, that “sometimes [you] gotta do a terrible thing for the greater good.” But, as the end of his life draws near, he sees from the other side. He advises his young, naïve friend: “Any time you see a man in uniform … kill him.”

So much for bothsidesism. Spoken by a man seeking to undo all that he has set in motion, Chris’s words are not enough to change the course of history, and he knows it. But as a piece of art, Wild Horse Nine is a powerful work of cinematic intelligence, McDonagh having given us a period piece that feels all too much of the present.

items.title: The Cooler-Than-You-Think History Behind the Kansas We Saw Tuesday
items.content_text:
“Kansas, get ready to learn what a polycule is,” read one Tuesday night tweet. All in due time. Let Kansans rest up. (This includes the ethically nonmonogamous community in Lawrence.)

Kansas must be exhausted. It swung left 21.06 points Tuesday. As everyone now knows, the state elected Adam Hamilton, a recent Democratic convert and founding pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, as its first Democratic U.S. senator since 1932. But it also appears to have chosen Cindy Holscher, an economic populist, as governor. Democrats picked up 20 seats in the statehouse, breaking the 16-year-old veto-proof Republican supermajority.

Giving birth to something new is always a bloodbath. So right now, the state is postpartum.

At the same time, Kansas likes a change. The state was forged in rebellion, and Kansans regularly break hard against anyone who’s exploiting them. Thomas Frank’s bellwether 2004 book What’s the Matter With Kansas? is misremembered as a cautionary tale of a moderate state that got waylaid by conservative Christianity. It’s really about a state that sacrificed its native radicalism to culture wars and trickle-down economics.

But repressed radicalism returns, evidently. As the home of Appeal to Reason (1895–1922), the largest-circulation socialist newspaper in American history, Kansas is also the birthplace of campaigns against oligarchs. In the 1890s, popular fury at railroads, banks, and grain-elevator operators drove the founding of the state’s Farmers’ Alliance and People’s Party. A version of this platform is what Holscher, the granddaughter of tenant farmers, campaigned on. She called for a complete moratorium on data centers, and an end to tariffs and the war in Iran, which have walloped the state’s farmers who risk bankruptcy as prices for fuel, fertilizer, and machine parts surge.

The same don’t-tread-on-me-ism extends to reproductive health in Kansas. In 2022, just after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, Kansans soundly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to ban abortion. Hamilton, who once described himself as “pro-life with a heavy heart,” is now explicitly pro-choice. “I acknowledge there is a moral tension surrounding the topic of abortion,” he has said, “but I do not believe that politicians should be making these decisions for women.” Last week, Rob Schenk, a former Operation Rescue leader and onetime anti-abortion militant in Kansas, endorsed Hamilton and praised his pro-choice views in the pages of Mother Jones. (Mary Harris “Mother” Jones was a frequent contributor to Appeal to Reason.)

Kansas Republicans were historically progressive or moderate, and they regularly supported the state’s many Democratic governors. But in the 1970s, the rich Koch network, which is headquartered in Wichita, began amassing right-wing influence. In 2012, the network helped oust moderate legislators in the state, and far-right Senator Sam Brownback, the Kochs’ made man, then pushed for deep tax cuts, notably to education. These cuts were so deep that the Kansas Supreme Court ruled that the state had failed in its legal duty to educate children.

In 2017, over Brownback’s veto, Republicans finally voted with Democrats to roll back the cuts. In 2018, four GOP legislators even defected to the Democrats, saying their party had become too complicit with Donald Trump. “Brownback” became shorthand for the MAGA catastrophe. During this election season, incumbent Democratic Governor Laura Kelly campaigned for Holscher, warning that her Republican opponent in the race, Ty Masterson, would take Kansas “back to Brownback.”

And then there’s Kansas’s origin story, perhaps the most vivid in the nation. Bleeding Kansas earned its moniker in 1854 when 5,000 pro-slavery terrorists from Missouri invaded the territory, brandishing Bowie fighting blades expressly designed for concussive chops and deep thrusts. They menaced voters at the polls, hijacked elections, and installed themselves in an illegitimate, pro-slavery legislature.

But after the Border Ruffians sacked Lawrence, which had been founded by abolitionists, Free-State Kansans rallied, notably John Brown and his sons, who slashed up five pro-slavery settlers with broadswords in May 1856. Kansas entered the union as a free state in 1861, pledged to the party of Lincoln. To go full wonk on you, Kansas voters have never, in the entire history of the state, elected a Democrat to a full Senate term by popular vote who didn’t already hold the seat by appointment of the governor. Senator-elect Adam Hamilton is the first Kansas Democrat to win a full term from scratch, via the popular ballot, without the benefit of incumbency by prior appointment.

For most of Tuesday night, Hamilton led in unofficial counts against the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall (an anti-abortion obstetrician who once sued 700 of his female patients for unpaid debts at 18 percent interest and had 81 of them arrested), but his lead shrank as the night wore on. When the AP called the race, Hamilton had 51 percent to Marshall’s 45 percent. “This election is a rebuke of unkindness and cruelty in Washington,” Hamilton said in his acceptance speech in Overland Park.

The election was also a rebuke of the party that has made unkindness and cruelty its stock-in-trade. Old habits die hard, party affiliations too. Just after his victory was announced, Hamilton claimed that “hundreds of thousands of Republicans” had voted for him. The numbers aren’t in yet, but this is not out of the question.

Thomas Frank is circumspect. He’s wary of Democrats. “It’s a whole lot better than Brownbackism or Trumpism, of course,” he told me. “And it was nice to see Marshall’s effort to use the culture wars to cancel people’s economic anxieties—the classic Kansas pattern—fail so completely.”

Hamilton, who studied at the Divinity School at Southern Methodist University, is about to join quite a club of freshman senators in D.C. He and Presbyterian seminarian James Talarico, senator-elect from Texas, will have a lot to talk about. Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, another religious man (he identifies as a “practicing Muslim”) with advanced degrees, will surely have something to add. But if the cool leftists in Congress ever privately doubt whether Hamilton, with his Ned Flanders–like affect, is rad enough to hang with them, they should fire up “Jesus, Protest, and Repentance,” the 2020 sermon Hamilton gave a few days after the murder of George Floyd.

Hamilton’s tone is mild, but his message is—well, it falls shy of John Brown, but it might have worked as an op-ed in Appeal to Reason. Expressing compassion for even the rowdiest protesters, Hamilton cites Dr. King: “Riots are the language of the unheard.” He says Colin Kaepernick was right, and that Christians must be committed to racial justice. He also shows off an impressive memento: the 1942 rookie card for Satchel Paige, the pride of Kansas City.

This is the sermon that Vice President JD Vance dragged incoherently in September, as he stumped for Marshall. Hamilton, Vance said, believes “it’s a sin to be white and a sin to raise cattle and eat meat.” Vance was bluffing as usual. But Kansans paid him no mind. And a few weeks later they voted Marshall, and MAGA, down.

items.title: If Democrats Can Tell the Right Story, They’ll Keep Winning
items.content_text:
Well before the final tally of the 2026 midterms had been registered, begun, the Narrative War had. As far as the White House was concerned, Tuesday wasn’t a verdict on President Trump. It was a brief, almost spasmodic reaction by voters to an uptick in gas prices—which, supposedly, would soon go down again.

The result, Trump insisted, wasn’t “a hit on me.” He conceded that the war with Iran played a part in the GOP’s drubbing, reasonable man that he is, but then minimized its role as much as possible.

The war “drove the gasoline up a little bit,” he granted, but then added, without evidence, that this was merely in the “short term.” Soon-to-be-former House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile, opted for an even more fatalistic interpretation, saying Republicans would have had to “defy more than a century of midterm history” to hold the House. (It is true that the party that takes the White House tends to fare poorly in the subsequent midterms, but there is an appreciable difference between “faring poorly” and experiencing, as outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis called the election, “an extinction-level event.” )

At any rate, the subtext was clear: Neither Trump nor MAGA had been rejected on any fundamental level. The outcome was either the will of history, per Johnson, or, per Trump, an example of voters throwing a tantrum in response to a supposedly temporary inconvenience. Either way, both implied, the electorate would soon return to MAGA Republicans.

Democrats, of course, were telling a different story: By their reckoning, the election showed that American voters had decisively and definitively rejected Trump and MAGA, period. There would be no going back.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to soon become the first Black speaker of the House in U.S. history, called the results “a stunning rebuke for MAGA extremism.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who is likely to once again be master of the Senate, this time at the head of a much larger caucus than during the Biden years, declared that “the days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over.” And Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, who won a smashing reelection and is widely seen as a potential 2028 front-runner, said that “in sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame-duck President Donald J. Trump.”

Now, at this point, you might expect me to adjudicate which one of these narratives is “correct.” But the truth about elections—and especially wave elections—is that their results can never be reduced into a single cause. Millions of people across a vast continent voted; no individual explanation could possibly encompass all of their motivations. So, yes, voters gave the GOP a shellacking because they were furious about gas prices and inflation. And, yes, voters gave the GOP a thumpin’ because they were sick and tired of MAGA’s lawlessness, authoritarianism, and corruption.

This may sound vexing, and I’m sure that pundits and anxious Democratic backbenchers will be providing gossip rags like Axios with endless “Dems in disarray” content as they try to navigate between these two narrative shoals. But I have good news for Democrats, if they’re willing to listen. And it comes from that most unlikely of sources, at least as far as good news is concerned: Hannah Arendt.

In the Trump era, Arendt has been quoted endlessly on the subject of political lying, which is fair enough; no one has written about the subject with more intelligence or contempt. But in “Truth and Politics,” an essay she published in The New Yorker in 1967, she explained why these two human concepts—the truth and politics—are actually frenemies at best. The gist of her argument was that politics is a realm where opinion and emotion, and not facts, reign supreme.

Naturally, that doesn’t mean it’s OK to straight-up lie. It simply means that any clear-eyed politician has to understand that their job is to take the facts and create a story about what they mean. As she put it, “Facts inform opinions, and opinions, inspired by different interests and passions, can differ widely and still be legitimate as long as they respect factual truth.”

For Arendt, facts and opinions, “though they must be kept apart, are not antagonistic to each other; they belong to the same realm.” A fact (her example is Germany’s invasion of Belgium in August 1914) “acquires political implications only by being put in an interpretative context.” Whoever reports what happened, she wrote, “always tells a story, and in this story the particular facts lose their contingency and acquire some humanly comprehensible meaning.”

It’s nicer to think, of course, that politics is simply about presenting people with empirical observations and allowing them to use their own powers of reason to draw the right conclusions. But Arendt warns, correctly, that when left on their own, “the mere telling of facts” results in “no action whatever; it even tends, under normal circumstances, toward the acceptance of things as they are.” Facts without narrative create confusion, paralysis, or even fatalism. It’s only when they’re used to tell a fact-based story that collective action becomes possible. It may be true that, as the far right likes to chortle, “facts don’t care about your feelings.” But that’s only because facts don’t care about anything. Facts don’t do anything. They have no agency; they’re just facts.

But when people, with all their feelings and opinions and capacity for action, are empowered with a fact-based story, it turns out that facts and feelings can get along very well indeed.

What does that mean, translated from Arendt-speak to the grubby language of partisan politics? It means that Democrats not only do not have to choose between the two competing narratives to “explain” the election but that they should positively refuse to do so. In the name of offering a story that provides that “interpretive context” Arendt calls for, Democrats can—and, indeed, as politicians, must—braid facts from both of these narratives together into a story of their own making and for their own purposes.

There’s one story that does this better than any other: anti-corruption. To many voters, it is the explanation for why gas costs so much; why inflation endures; why education, housing, and health care have become so expensive; and especially why they feel like they can’t get ahead. In an NBC News exit poll, 90 percent said government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their vote. And in Trump, they see corruption incarnate: CBS News, meanwhile, found that about six in 10 voters think Trump puts his own personal interests over the country’s.

Many of the Democratic Party’s most respected strategists have been saying as much already. “The candidates who have been most successful are the ones who have tied the cost of corruption to the cost of living,” Celinda Lake told The Christian Science Monitor last week. And Jesse Ferguson summed up the shift for Politico: “Democrats used to talk about corruption as a crime. Now corruption is the explanation for costs.”

There’s a recent international example of this approach working—spectacularly—as well. After more than 15 years of Viktor Orbán’s kleptocratic authoritarianism, Hungarian voters voted earlier this year in overwhelming numbers for Péter Magyar’s Tisza party, which ran a campaign that, as one analysis put it, set out to negate “Orbán’s populist, anti-elitist politics by focusing on corruption.” Magyar didn’t ask Hungarians to choose between their democracy and “kitchen-table” issues. He told them they were one and the same, and the voters agreed.

That is what Arendt meant when she argued that organizing people together to change the world—that is to say, doing politics—requires an approach that rejects outright lying while also avoiding a complacent expectation that “the truth” will reveal itself for voters to follow. The narrative wars have begun. If Democrats are smart, they’ll opt for storytelling instead.

items.title: Did Data Centers Make the Difference for Democrats?
items.content_text:
Democrats expected these midterms would be good for them. What they got was nothing short of a blowout. So far, the party has secured 54 Senate seats and 259 in the House, sailing to its biggest congressional landslide in half a century. If Democrats’ lead holds in states that are still counting ballots, 75 percent of the country will live in a state with a Democratic governor. More than half will live in states where Democrats control both the governor’s mansion and the legislature.

The flashiest contest this cycle certainly wasn’t the race for New Jersey’s 2nd congressional district, spanning most of the southern part of the state. And yet it has a few features that showcase the strength of a blue tsunami that stretched well beyond national headlines. For years, the district was represented nationally by a relatively moderate Republican. Then, in 2018, it flipped to Democrat Jeff Van Drew. The next year, Van Drew became a Republican and pledged his “undying support” to President Trump. The change seemed to track with the district’s rightward-shifting politics. Van Drew was reelected by a 17-point margin in 2024, when New Jersey’s 2nd congressional district swung for Trump by 15 points. With that history, he seemed poised to sail to a comfy reelection this year. Last month, nevertheless, the House Democrats’ campaign arm, the DCCC, added the race to its “districts in play” list and poured in $1.5 million. Van Drew was still expected to easily best his Democratic challenger, Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock. Instead, he lost by three points.

How did the upset happen, and did it have anything to do with the much-maligned data center being built in the heart of the district? Behind thick walls, the concrete firm Northeast Precast and DataOne Vineland—the local subsidiary of a European company—is erecting an AI data center for Nebius, a so-called “neocloud” provider responsible for designing the facility, sourcing the chips, and stewarding its racks and servers. Per the terms of a deal worth up to $19 billion, the end buyer of DataOne Vineland’s computing power will be Microsoft. As I wrote this summer, the project has attracted intense opposition from Cumberland County residents, who have turned up by the hundreds to newly rowdy City Council and planning meetings.

“I think everyone was kind of shocked,” said Matt Williams, a co-founder of SustainSJ, which has spearheaded local organizing against DataOne Vineland. In addition to Mullock’s surprise win against Van Drew, Democrats swept the sheriff’s and county commissioners’ race in Cumberland County, where the data center is located. “People just drew a hard line,” he said, and wanted change “regardless of political affiliation.” In the lead-up to Election Day, Williams said, he saw “Republicans for Mullock” signs dotting yards.

He’s hopeful that the blue wave will create a friendlier environment for the group’s ongoing fight against the data center. In August, an investigation by Floodlight News and The Guardian found that DataOne Vineland had been operating dozens of gas generators without permits from the state’s environmental regulator. New Jersey’s Department of Environmental Protection then issued a $1.1 million fine and demanded the facility apply for the necessary permits or cease operations by November 6. The project’s developers are contesting the fine, arguing that they don’t need permits. They’ve reportedly continued operating generators as they install gas fuel cells. In recent days, residents have reported that noise emanating from the site is louder than ever.

It’s not hard to connect Van Drew’s loss to residents’ unhappiness with the data center. One of the data center’s developers had called Van Drew’s support for the project “critical” to its being able to get off the ground. Its investors donated to his campaign. And while Van Drew eventually walked back his public support for the project, Mullock dinged him on the campaign trail over it. “My opponent has sold out South Jersey to data centers, to the war in Iran, to doubling our health insurance prices, all for a pathetic undying support to Donald Trump,” Mullock said in the opening statement of his debate with Van Drew last month.

Nationwide, data centers and broader debates around AI were a hot issue this cycle. All but one of the at least 41 local ballot questions to ban data centers and take away their tax breaks passed by healthy margins this election. In case the scale of voters’ repudiation didn’t land the first time: No fewer than 40 of 41 data center restrictions passed. Insurer Allianz now predicts that 47 gigawatts’ worth of planned data center projects are at risk from Democratic governors who’ve backed full or conditional moratoria. In Downe Township, which is also in Cumberland County, 87 percent of voters responded “no” to a nonbinding ballot question asking if they “support data centers” being built there. More than 100 New Jersey municipalities have already banned them.

Democrats looked to tap into that ire at the ballot box. The DCCC pushed for ads targeting Republicans’ records on data centers and AI in nearly half of the races it targeted. NJ-2 was not among them. Mullock certainly hasn’t been shy about where he stands on DataOne Vineland. “I feel really strongly that Vineland got duped and these people got left behind, and you have a company that’s clearly polluting the area and has been fined,” he told me. Yet while Mullock reasons that stance certainly helped win support in Cumberland County—where his vote share was strongest—he isn’t sure how much of a factor it was in his victory overall.

Mullock said the top question he got over the course of the campaign was, “Will you be a decent human being?” Affordability concerns, he believed, were a distant second. Many voters also complained about the Iran war. To the extent that data center fights contributed to his win, Mullock suspects it was thanks to the many issues wrapped up in them, including voters’ concerns about money in politics, corruption, how to regulate artificial intelligence, and the money and power concentrated in Big Tech. “It even gets to the president—his statements on not regulating AI, and the people he chooses to have sitting behind him at his inauguration,” Mullock told me, referencing the coterie of Silicon Valley billionaires who attended the event in 2024. “That says something. Clearly there was a rebuke.”

If these elections were a rebuke of Trump, they were also a referendum on the company he keeps. Just a few years ago, Silicon Valley executives cast themselves as do-gooder liberals who opposed Trump and cared about things like climate change. Just two years into those billionaires’ love affair with MAGA, polling has found that most voters think of tech CEOs as Republicans and of tech companies as the biggest corporate spenders on GOP campaigns. The party didn’t seem to benefit much politically from its associations with Silicon Valley this cycle. Exit polling shows voters trust Democrats more to handle the economy, foreign policy, health care, government corruption, and policies about transgender people. Data centers and AI weren’t top issues for voters on Tuesday, but 57 percent said those technologies will do more to hurt society than help. Seventy-six percent said they opposed building data centers in their communities. Despite the nearly $500 million Elon Musk poured into the midterms on behalf of Republicans, the party suffered some of its biggest losses in living memory.

Hyperscalers now have to reckon with the reputational consequences of having jumped into bed with Trump. Facing prospective material consequences, companies like OpenAI are scrambling to align their messaging with the new political reality. A post-midterms missive from OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane name-drops Franklin Delano Roosevelt and urges aspiring Democratic presidential candidates to embrace “an affirmative, big idea that puts people back in control—not by shielding them from AI but by helping them use it to reclaim agency over their lives.” Democrats may not be so easily convinced that OpenAI—whose president poured millions into MAGA Inc. and GOP candidates this cycle—has their best interest at heart.

As this week’s results show, Democrats may not need tech oligarchs on their side to win big. Centrists, by contrast, have been arguing that their party spent the Biden era being too tough on Big Tech—that overzealous antitrust enforcement, “faculty lounge populism,” and personal snubs had mistakenly alienated Democrats from corporate allies that had helped them win since the 1980s. A group funded by OpenAI—along with Amazon, a16z, and Flock Safety—has made the case that Democrats need to get back in Silicon Valley’s good graces. The Chamber of Progress’s Blue Horizon Project argued earlier this year that if the Democratic Party hopes to “rebuild our coalition and reclaim our legacy as the party of innovation,” it will have to “reset” its relationship with the technology sector.

After an election where Democrats secured historic margins while tearing into Big Tech, the Chamber of Progress has somewhat frantically contended that the election actually had very little to do with that. Like climate change, the group’s executive director, Adam Kovacevich, points out, data centers and AI in this election were what pollsters call a “low salience” issue, i.e., far down on their list of priorities. Data centers, though—which are broadly unpopular—do seem to be an uncomfortably loud and hyperlocal manifestation of lots of things voters care quite a lot about, including income and wealth distribution. The fact that tech industry spending has become so singularly focused on a uniquely resource-intensive model of machine learning development, moreover, has also given its executive a very different set of material interests than they had even during the Obama administration. In their endless hunt for land and electrons, hyperscalers like OpenAI have become fossil fuel–guzzling real estate developers demanding tax breaks and preferential regulatory treatment. It makes sense that their billionaire executives have embraced Republicans too.

Mullock, whose race received backing from the centrist Blue Dog PAC, strongly supports his new colleagues’ calls to subpoena Big Tech CEOs and data center developers. “When you have a president who’s saying that there are no guardrails—that they should come up with the guardrails themselves—that should be disturbing,” he said. And when it comes to AI, Mullock added, “we don’t have a full understanding of what could or could not happen. To me it’s common sense that our elected officials need to have a very clear understanding of where we stand.”

The question after this year’s midterms isn’t whether Democrats need to say nice things about Silicon Valley CEOs in order to win big majorities; clearly they don’t. The party will, however, have to figure out how to deliver for voters who see those executives’ data centers as big, ugly symbols of an economy that makes billionaires richer and their lives more expensive. Here’s hoping it can.

items.title: The New House Will Have Genuine Working-Class People. Will It Matter?
items.content_text:
The 2026 midterms were a referendum on President Trump’s economy, but anyone who says that means only gas and grocery prices has misread the mood. From data centers to the Trump family raking in billions to the corruption at the center of the ballroom construction site Trump spoke from, the day after the election, the results were a rejection of the idea that billionaires and the companies they run can do anything they want and can pay politicians to do anything they want. Voters didn’t just want to go back to the pre-Trump status quo: They wanted to see a real change in the political economy of this country.

You can see that in progressive victories up and down the ballot across the country, including in the election of rank-and-file union members, not the lawyers or political nepobabies or children of wealth who usually occupy such seats.

“I think historically unions have backed Democrats and Republicans for a long time across the country,” said Neidi Dominguez, executive director of Organized Power In Numbers, a group that helped plan May Day demonstrations around the country this year. “But being backed by workers and then being a worker yourself is not the same thing.… They don’t need a staffer to give them a talking point about the power that it is to have a union and have collective power as a worker. That’s powerful.”

Of at least 17 union members likely to be sworn in as Democrats in Congress next year, 12 turned red districts blue. In Pennsylvania’s 7th congressional district, for example, firefighter Bob Brooks beat incumbent Republican Ryan Mackenzie by 12 points. “I’ve spoken with people across the Lehigh Valley throughout this campaign who are playing the game the best they can,” he said at his victory speech. “Working hard, punching the clock, doing everything right, and they’re still struggling to get ahead or just get by. They’re sick and tired of waking up every day and getting kicked in the teeth by a broken political system that has left them behind.”

He went through the laundry list of financial burdens crushing working families, but he didn’t just promise relief. He promised a change. “We aren’t going down there to try and piece things back together the way they were before,” he said. “We’re going down there to shake up the status quo, fight for working people, stop the bullshit, and build something better from the ashes.”

Across the border in Ohio, another union member, ironworker Brian Poindexter, beat Republican incumbent Max Miller in his 7th congressional district race. But the Rust Belt won’t be the only region to send workers and union members to Congress next year. New York State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez, who joined a union when she started working for Columbia University and has said her union work helped get her into politics, carried New York’s heavily Democratic 7th district with more than 83 percent of the vote. Rebecca Cooke, a waitress and small-business owner who grew up on a dairy farm and started a nonprofit to help women entrepreneurs, is projected to win Wisconsin’s 3rd congressional district by just over six points, defeating an extremely MAGA opponent. Trump won her district all three times he ran for president. In Texas’s 23rd district, which encompasses Uvalde, site of a tragic 2022 school shooting, former public school teacher Katy Padilla Stout is projected to win by eight points. Former smoke jumper Sam Forstag is also projected to win Montana’s new 1st congressional district by three points.

And, of course, in the closely watched Texas and Michigan Senate races, James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed were once union members. In Maine, fifth-generation logger Troy Jackson ended Republican Susan Collins’s three-decade career in Washington, D.C., likely defeating her by seven points. “If you’re watching this after getting home from a shift or sitting at the table wondering how you’re going to pay the next bill, I want you to hear something very clearly,” he said in his victory speech. “You are sending somebody to Washington who knows exactly what that feels like.”  

These working people also owe their victories to working people. Democrats won union and nonunion households alike, but they won households with at least two members overwhelmingly, 64 to 34 percent, according to exit polls. The party won every income level, including households making under $50,000 a year by 57 to 41 percent. When it comes to the education divide, the only group Republicans won a majority of were voters who had only a high school education. It was also a win for representation: About half the country is working class, but only 5 percent of members of Congress are.

As Brooks said, they ran not just to get things done—they ran to shake up the system, and the Democratic Party.


What all of these candidates have in common is that they promised to use their union histories to fight for working people in Washington. They said during their campaigns they want to raise wages and make health care more affordable for families. What helping working families means beyond that, exactly, may vary a bit. Valdez is a college-educated progressive in far-left New York City, while other members of this new working-people coalition are representing more moderate districts.

There’s some evidence their backgrounds will make a difference. “Working-class people face significant hurdles running for office, but when they win, they vote in more pro-worker ways than their upper-class counterparts, and use the rhetoric to match it,” said Todd Tucker, director of the industrial policy and trade program at the Roosevelt Institute. If they want to draft good policies, they should focus on hiring staff with the same priorities, he added.

The new union members will also be part of the larger Democratic Party that must decide how its new majorities—at least 54 seats in the Senate and 245 in the House, but with more wins possible—will govern. House Minority Leader and soon-to-be first Black House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made conciliatory noises on Morning Joe Wednesday, promising to concentrate on affordability. But CNN is reporting that those close to him say he plans to go after CEOs and tax the rich, promising a new era of populism. “The American people are rightly frustrated. They want disruption, they want dramatic change,” Jeffries told CNN.

On that score, he is right. In almost every cycle since the Trump era began in 2016, voters have chosen change, even voting for Trump when they didn’t like or agree with him in 2024, in part because he kept promising to dismantle the system. The system they want dismantled is the one that feels unfair, the one that makes the American dream a broken promise, whoever is trying to achieve it and wherever they live.

Anger about the fundamental unfairness of the economy has been building for years, but voters have been dissatisfied with both parties on their ability to deliver. That’s where next year needs to be different if the Democratic Party wants to use its majority to make working people’s lives better.

There are a lot of policies that could help working people that Democrats have long said they support—like increasing the minimum wage and making it easier to join a union—that they’ve yet to get over the finish line, especially to improve wages. The new working-class members of Congress could make these policies priorities. “Wages are very real to them, and I do think there has been a lack of like real awareness that wages are part of the affordability equation,” said Celine McNicholas, director of policy at the Economic Policy Institute, a progressive think tank in Washington, D.C. 

The fact that these elected officials were in unions also means that they are used to organizing and working with other workers, said Sharon Block, executive director of the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University School of Law. “Being in a union is a collective activity,” she said. “They are engaging with working people in a way that probably a lot of members of Congress don’t regularly.” Enhancing workers’ ability to join unions would also potentially increase the pool of union members who jump into elected office in the future.

There are changes set to happen next year, like reductions in Medicaid coverage and increases in health care premiums, that will need to be addressed as soon as possible. There are long-term increases in caregiving and education costs, too often left out of affordability discussions, but which people who are used to stretching a paycheck know are more immediate problems to be addressed.

Voters see these not as disparate evils, but a result of the overarching concentration of power at the top. “This is not just about us, like having a sort of silver-bullet policy or one thing, but we need to shift the dynamics of power and unionization and easing the path toward organizing workplaces as a way to really get at those deep structures of power,” said Kate Bahn, the chief economist at the Institute for Women’s Policy Research, a nonprofit research organization. “So when we take trends like AI being integrated into workplaces, or rising health care costs, and things like that, unions shape those dynamics, and so even if it’s a policy area outside of just labor law, having the presence of unions really changes those things.”

Mike Pierce, the executive director of Protect Borrowers, a debt research and advocacy group, also pointed to Talarico’s Senate campaign in Texas, during which he spoke about what it was like when he was younger and struggling with debt, including medical and student loan debt. As a result, he’s supported debt relief and been critical of big credit card companies and banks, he said. “Moving beyond labor priorities, there are economic priorities that these lawmakers share, along with this generation of economic populists that just got swept in, that’s everything from checking concentrated corporate power by taxing billionaires and big corporations,” Pierce said.
